_meta.purpose: Canonical content blocks for the OSCI Pro PDF report. Each subscale has two frames: strength (when the subscale is a relative high point for the respondent) and development (when it's a relative low point). The report generator selects the right frame at render time. Voice follows OSCI_Feedback_Style_guide.

courteously_charismatic.label: The Courteously Charismatic
courteously_charismatic.tagline: Competent and connected. The next work is consistency.
courteously_charismatic.opening_paragraph: You sit in the part of the model where most leaders would like to be, with Confidence and Social Skills both working for you. People in this position tend to be both respected and liked, which is harder to combine than the literature usually admits. The opportunity here is rarely about finding what you do well. It is about keeping it steady, across different audiences and under pressure.
courteously_charismatic.what_the_quadrant_means: Courteously Charismatic is the version of the model where presence and warmth land together. You are credible in the room. People listen when you speak and trust what you say. The risk that comes with this position is invisible to most people in it. Because the conventional charisma signals are working for you, you may not notice the moments when they slip, and other people often do not tell you. The work in this quadrant is the work of consistency: closing the gap between your best version and your average one. That is what the Charismatic Consistency Index, and the development areas in this report, are pointing at.
courteously_charismatic.common_blind_spots: Two patterns recur for people in this quadrant. The first is variable presence: a noticeable difference between the version of you that turns up at 9am and the version at 4pm, or between the version that turns up for senior people and the version that turns up for everyone else. The second is the assumption that because you are good at this on a good day, the work is done. The development pages in this report identify the specific places where the work continues.

unknowingly_influential.label: The Unknowingly Influential
unknowingly_influential.opening_paragraph: You sit in the part of the model where social skill is strong and confidence sometimes struggles to keep pace. People in this position are often liked, trusted, and listened to. They can also be overlooked when credit is being shared out, often because they underestimate the influence they already have. The influence is real. The opportunity is to see it as clearly as others do.
unknowingly_influential.what_the_quadrant_means: The Unknowingly Influential is one of the more interesting positions in the model. Other people often experience you as someone they want to work with, take advice from, and have in the room. Many people in this position experience themselves as not quite stepping up. The gap between those two readings is the main opportunity available to you. Closing it does not mean becoming louder. It means trusting that what you are already doing is working, and being willing to claim space proportionate to the value you bring.
unknowingly_influential.common_blind_spots: Two patterns recur here. The first is over-deferring: holding back a view because you assume someone more senior or more confident will offer a better one, when the room actually wanted yours. The second is under-claiming: describing your contribution to a piece of work in terms so modest that nobody else realises what you did. The development pages in this report will probably touch on assertiveness and self-esteem. Both are the work of bringing your external impact and your internal sense of yourself into alignment.

occasionally_overconfident.label: The Occasionally Overconfident
occasionally_overconfident.tagline: Commands attention. The opportunity is warmth and restraint.
occasionally_overconfident.opening_paragraph: You sit in the part of the model where confidence is strong and social skill is the area with most room to grow. People in this position usually walk into the room well, and presence is rarely the problem. The opportunity is in what happens after that, in the moments where warmth, restraint, or attention to the other person can produce a better outcome than another assertion.
occasionally_overconfident.what_the_quadrant_means: Occasionally Overconfident is a position that often comes with strong delivery skills. You are not short on conviction. The cost of that strength is that conviction can crowd out the quieter behaviours that build long-term influence: noticing what the other person is bringing, leaving space for them to find their own answer, sharing credit specifically, admitting where you do not know. The development pages in this report will probably point at one or more of those. The work is not to be less confident. It is to add the moves that complete the picture.
occasionally_overconfident.common_blind_spots: Two patterns recur here. The first is dominating the conversational space without realising: more airtime than the situation needs, more certainty than the situation warrants. The second is missing the cumulative cost of small moments where warmth would have been the better move. Both are recoverable. Neither requires a personality transplant. The activities in this report are about adding moves, not subtracting from who you are.

incidentally_invisible.label: The Incidentally Invisible
incidentally_invisible.tagline: Capable and sometimes overlooked. The gap to close is visibility, not ability.
incidentally_invisible.opening_paragraph: You sit in the part of the model where both Confidence and Social Skills have room to grow. People in this position are often capable, often hard-working, and sometimes invisible to the people whose attention would help them most. The gap is rarely ability. It is visibility. The work here can be the most rewarding in the model, because the distance between current and possible is the widest.
incidentally_invisible.what_the_quadrant_means: Incidentally Invisible is a position that can be misread as a verdict. It is not. It is a starting point. Many of the people who reach the Courteously Charismatic quadrant started somewhere closer to this one and did the work over time. The two priority subscales in this report are where to start. Pick one. Work on it for four to six weeks. Then come back to the other. The instrument and the report are designed for exactly this kind of incremental, visible improvement.
incidentally_invisible.common_blind_spots: The pattern that recurs here is treating the position as fixed rather than as the current state of a developable system. People in this quadrant often describe themselves as 'not naturally good at this kind of thing', and that framing closes the door before any work can begin. The framing the rest of this report uses is different: charisma is a set of specific skills, each one improvable on its own, with practice that can be done in real working situations. The activities are designed to be done in the next four weeks, not someday.

A1.name: Self-Esteem and Self-Worth

strength.what_this_suggests: Your Self-Esteem score sits in a strong range. The pattern this points to is a settled internal baseline that does not move much with the most recent event. You can take a piece of criticism, weigh what is useful in it, and not let it reshape your view of who you are. You can take a good outcome without needing it to confirm your worth. The baseline holds.
strength.why_it_matters: Settled self-esteem is the platform everything else stands on. When the baseline is steady, you can hear hard feedback without flinching, give difficult feedback without performing humility, take a setback without an identity collapse, and bring views that may be unpopular without needing the room to validate them first. Most of the harder behaviours later in this report depend on this one being in place.
strength.how_to_use_it_even_better: The strength to develop further is not your self-esteem itself, but its visible effect on others. People who are settled in themselves tend to put other people at ease. You can use that deliberately. In meetings where the room is anxious, your steadiness changes the temperature. In conversations with someone who is wavering, your settled register helps them think more clearly. The opportunity is to notice these moments and make the most of them: when you walk into the room, you are bringing something the room can use.

development.what_this_score_tells_you:
A note on the concepts before we look at what the score means for you.

Self-esteem is one of the older measures in social psychology. The textbooks build it from three components: your view of who you are (self-concept), your view of how you physically present (self-image), and your sense of whether you are meeting the standards you have set for yourself (accomplishments). In working life, the third one usually does most of the work. Whether you like yourself in the moment, and whether you are living up to the standards you hold for yourself, is the version of self-esteem that affects how you operate at work.

Higher self-esteem at this band looks like a balanced view of your abilities and flaws, the ability to set boundaries that hold, and the resilience to come back from mistakes without unfair self-blame. Lower self-esteem looks like consistent self-criticism, avoidance of challenges, people-pleasing, and an underlying sense of not being quite good enough.

Now what this score is telling us in your case.

A lower score on this subscale often means you are more self-critical than you need to be, which is not helpful for you. Like spending too much time looking in the wrong kind of mirror. A 20x magnifying mirror in a hotel bathroom shows every blemish at a brutal scale. It is also useless for getting ready in the morning, because it cannot show you how you actually look. Your eyebrows are magnificent at 20x, but you cannot see the fact that you forgot to button up your trousers. Lower levels of self-esteem can start with the habit of checking yourself in a critical mirror, several times a day, and walking away each time feeling a little worse than you did before.
development.what_it_costs_to_leave_this_alone: Low self-esteem has an internal cost, and it shows up externally. You hold back a view you would otherwise have brought. You read a piece of feedback on your work as if it were feedback on you, which makes it harder to hear and use. You give other people's assessments of your contribution more weight than your own. You miss your own strengths and contribution. Over time, the people around you adjust to the slightly uncertain version of you, and that version becomes the one they expect. The cycle persists, and gets harder to interrupt.
development.how_to_close_the_gap:
The skill to build is what the book calls being in good faith with yourself. The actor's version: you cannot show confidence without being in good faith with yourself first. Practically, the real work is in changing that damn mirror. The full-length one shows a broader view of how you showed up today, with no cruel magnification required. Most of what you are doing on an average day is fine. See that. Some of it is good. Focus on that. A small amount of it is better than anyone else around you could achieve, celebrate that. Only a full-length mirror lets you see all three. The 20x mirror only ever shows the worst. Other people's view of your work, asked for carefully and listened to, is one of the most accurate mirrors available to you.

Self-esteem is foundation work. It rarely shifts by being addressed directly. It shifts when you give yourself enough evidence to update the internal version, and the evidence comes from doing the work in real situations.
where_you_might_start: At the end of each week, name three moments from the week where you would still respect what you did if nobody had been watching. Not three wins. Three moments. The criterion is the standard you hold for yourself when nobody else is in the room, and you keep it. This is the full-length mirror in practice. The list is the evidence for the version of yourself that the magnifying mirror keeps hiding.

When something goes badly, separate the incident from the verdict. The meeting did not go well. That is the incident. "I am to blame" is a jail sentence, and you have not given yourself a fair trial. Diagnose the actual thing, look at the arguments for the prosecution and the defence, identify anything you could do differently or better next time, fix the specific bit, and move on. The automatic jump from incident to verdict, where you get the blame, is just the miserable magnifying mirror doing its dreadful work. Smash it. Naming the two as separate, in the moment, is what stops the slide.

When you receive critical feedback, hold the response for twenty-four hours. Then come back to it and ask one question: what part of this is information I can use? The rest is noise. Most criticism contains a small useful core inside a larger emotional reaction. The day's pause for reflection lets the noise reduce, and lets you judge the criticism in the full-length mirror.

Use the Asking For Feedback Worth Getting method from the companion book with three people you trust. Specific ask: "What one thing could I do differently to be more effective for you?" Your own view of your work is one data point. When self-esteem is unreliable, it is rarely the most accurate one. Other people's specific observations are the way the picture corrects itself.

A1.subtitle: The settled internal baseline that does not move much with the most recent event.
A1.next_level_up: Moving up here means being less affected by the most recent thing that happened to you. The praise lands but does not inflate you. The criticism lands but does not derail you. The people around you experience someone who is more reliably themselves, and they relax in your company because the version of you they get is steadier than it used to be.
A1.where_it_helps: Where this helps you most: the weeks when the feedback is mixed. Praise and criticism both land in proportion, and the people around you get the same steady version either way.
A1.where_gain_shows: Where the gain will show first: the view you would otherwise hold back. A steadier internal baseline tends to bring more of your contribution into the room.

A2.name: Resilience and Composure

strength.what_this_suggests: Your Resilience and Composure score sits in a strong range. You stay functional under pressure. When meetings start going wrong, you can slow down rather than speed up. When something has gone wrong already, you can move from the event to what is now possible within a useful time window. The visible version of this is composure that does not require the suppression of feeling.
strength.why_it_matters: Staying calm when it matters is what lets the rest of your skills keep working. Most professional setbacks are not catastrophic in themselves. What does the damage is the reaction to them. People who stay composed are also the people who stay credible, because the room watches how they handle the difficult moment and updates its view accordingly.
strength.how_to_use_it_even_better: The opportunity is to be the calmer presence in a room that needs one. When others are struggling under pressure, your calm gives everyone else room to think. The deliberate use of this strength is to notice when a room is tilting toward panic and to be the steady voice that brings the temperature down. Not by minimising the problem. By staying with it long enough to make a useful decision.

development.what_this_score_tells_you:
A note on the concepts before we look at what the score means for you.

Resilience and Composure are two related skills that the questionnaire measures together. Composure is the in-the-moment skill: staying steady, clear-headed and in command when pressure starts to rise. Resilience is the after-the-fact skill: recovering from a setback in reasonable time, rather than carrying it like a wound, for days. The research literature on stress and emotion regulation treats them separately. Most people are better at one than the other.

Higher scores at this band describe someone who stays steady under pressure without suppressing what they feel, and who moves on from setbacks within a reasonable timeframe. People around them see someone who bends in difficult moments but does not break, and who gets back on track reliably and in good time. Lower scores at this band can show up in two distinct ways. The first is the person who handles the moment well at the time, but pays for it emotionally for days afterwards. The second is the person who recovers well from setbacks but freezes in the moment and loses access to their best thinking just when they need it most. Both possibilities exist in your subscale score. Read your own profile against the two and decide which is the bigger gap for you.

Now what this score is telling us in your case.

A lower score on this subscale does not usually mean you cannot handle pressure. Most people in this band handle far more pressure than they give themselves credit for. The gap is somewhere more specific. Either the field of attention narrows when the stakes rise, and what was an interaction with people becomes a struggle with the situation. Or you handle the moment cleanly, and the setback occupies your thoughts for longer than it should afterwards. Either pattern is a signal that the composure muscle or the resilience muscle, or both, has not yet been fully built.
development.what_it_costs_to_leave_this_alone: Pressure rises when the people around you are watching most carefully. The version of you that turns up in difficult moments is often the version they remember, and a difficult moment handled shakily can be paid for in reputation long after the moment itself is over. The cost of fragile composure can be that people downgrade their opinion of you against the easier moments where things are going well. The cost of fragile resilience is different. It is the cumulative weight of carrying setbacks longer than necessary, which over time can produce caution in you where decisiveness used to live. People around you might also notice your slow recovery before they consider the original setback, and adjust to the version of you they see, the one still managing the last thing.
development.how_to_close_the_gap:
The skill to build is two skills, and they respond to different work. Composure is built by slowing your own pace in the moment, deliberately, so that the incident does not pull you along with it. Like a pilot working through her standard operating procedures in a calm and measured way as the engine fails. The image we are seeking is the unrushed, measured response. The deliberate beat between noticing something is wrong and responding.

Resilience is built differently. When something has gone wrong, treat it the way you would treat your car not starting in the morning. Diagnose the actual problem. Do not get distracted by the consequences. Get help if you need it. Fix the specific thing. Learn from it. Move on. Notice that damning verdicts about your own competence or the cruelty of fate are not part of the protocol. A car that does not start is not a referendum on the car or the driver. A setback at work is not a referendum on you.

Three principles frame most approaches to pressure, and both skills lie downstream of them.

•  Nobody cares as much as you think they do. Do not overreact in the moment. •  Nobody is likely to die. This is not an emergency, and the consequences when put in context are usually much smaller than you think. •  Get over yourself. Yes, you matter. Yes, this is a challenging situation. But you are one of many billions of people in the world going through similar things on a daily basis. Holding that perspective frees up the attention you need to handle the situation.

Each one is in the methods at the back of this report.

Composure and resilience are built where they are needed, not in private. Each pressured moment you handle without collapsing into a verdict on yourself is one more piece of evidence that you can.
where_you_might_start: When you notice pressure rising, slow down by one beat before you respond. Just one. The slowdown breaks the speed-up cycle. It also signals to the world that you are still in control of yourself. The deliberate breath and pause to think is the easiest move you can make, and it works almost every time.

Before a high-stakes meeting, use the Five-Minutes Practice (page 16). Name what you are carrying into the room. Imagine what the room might need from this meeting that they may not have said. Choose the state you are going to bring. Reset the body. The practice is short. The effect is the gap between an interaction that drifts and one that lands.

After a setback, give yourself a finite window to feel what you feel about it. An hour. Half a day. Then move to the diagnostic question: what is the next useful action? The window allows the emotional reaction. The question starts the recovery. The window should be non-negotiable in both directions. Less than the window and you have not processed the thing, so any conclusions you make might be wrong in substance and reason. More than the window, and you are carrying it too long. Same result.

When something has gone wrong, treat it the way you would treat your car not starting. Get help if you need it. Mitigate any immediate consequences. Diagnose the actual problem. Fix the specific thing. Learn from it. Move on. Hurtful verdicts about your competence have no place in the protocol.

A2.subtitle: Staying functional under pressure, without suppressing what you feel.
A2.next_level_up: Moving up here means handling difficult moments with the room watching, and not paying for it for days afterwards. You stay in the conversation rather than freezing or escalating. You move on from setbacks within a useful window rather than carrying them. The people around you notice that you are the calmer presence when things get hard, and they bring more of their thinking to you because of it.
A2.where_it_helps: Where this helps you most: the moments after something goes wrong. While the room is still reacting, you are already working the problem, and people take their cue from that.
A2.where_gain_shows: Where the gain will show first: the meeting after the setback. Recovering visibly, and in good order, changes what the room expects of you under pressure.

A3.name: Assertiveness and Accountability

strength.what_this_suggests: Your Assertiveness score sits in a strong range. You say the thing that needs saying. You take responsibility for outcomes, including the ones that have not gone well. When you commit to something, you commit specifically, and the people around you know what to expect from you.
strength.why_it_matters: Assertive behaviour is the visible expression of self-respect and respect for others. People can act on what you say because you have said it clearly. People trust what you commit to because your commitments are specific. Over time, you become someone the room turns to when a difficult message needs to be delivered or a difficult decision needs to be made.
strength.how_to_use_it_even_better: The development edge for someone with strong assertiveness is calibration. The same directness that works well in most settings can land too hard in some. The skill to develop is reading the room's capacity for directness in the moment, and adjusting the volume without softening the message. The point is not to become less direct. It is to make directness land more reliably.

development.what_this_score_tells_you:
A note on the concepts before we look at what the score means for you.

Assertiveness and Accountability are two related skills the questionnaire measures together. Assertiveness, in the charismatic sense, is saying what needs to be said for everyone's benefit, in the kindest and most respectful way, even though it might be hard to hear or hard to say. The bar is what the room or the people need, not what you want. Accountability is the matching skill on the other side of a decision: owning the consequences of what you said or did not say, what you decided or did not decide. The two hold each other up. An assertive person who does not take accountability becomes the loudest voice that nobody trusts. An accountable person who is not assertive becomes the one who quietly takes the blame for the things they could have spoken up about earlier.

Higher scores in this subscale describe someone who says the difficult thing when the room needs to hear it, who is willing to be wrong in public, and who carries the consequences of their judgements without deflecting or disappearing. People around them know where they stand. Lower scores can show up in two distinct ways. The first is the person who does not say the difficult thing, lets the decision proceed without their view in it, and then carries the consequences anyway, and knows it. The second is the person who says the thing but delivers it so badly that it lands like a dead cat in the middle of the table: the intention was right, the construction or delivery was wrong, and the room moves on without engaging with it. Read your own profile against the two and decide which is the bigger gap for you.

Now what this score is telling us in your case.

A lower score on this subscale is usually less about courage than about preparation. Most people in this band are perfectly capable of saying the thing. What they are missing is a reliable way to construct it, and a reliable shape to put it inside. Without those, the default is silence, because silence is at least predictable. Either you are not on the record, or you are on the record badly. The work is the same in both cases. Saying the thing well, in a structure that gives the room a chance to receive it.
development.what_it_costs_to_leave_this_alone:
The cost of not being on the record is that the decision proceeds without your view in it, and you live with the consequences anyway. That is the quiet failure mode, with guilt attached, because you knew and didn't say. It compounds over time, and affects your sense of self as well as your reputation. People might stop asking what you think, because they have learned not to expect a useful answer. Your influence narrows to the things you are willing to fight for, which becomes a shrinking list, because each unsaid thing makes the next one harder to say.

The cost of saying the thing badly is louder. A message that lands like a dead cat tends to contaminate everything it touches. The room remembers the feeling and avoids the subject the next time it comes up, even when it needs to be discussed again. People who repeatedly fail to get their point across effectively, even though they had the courage to try, are not seen as brave. They are seen as the person who makes meetings worse. Both costs damage your standing in the room. They damage it in different directions, but the damage is the same shape.
development.how_to_close_the_gap:
The skill to build is two skills, working together. The first is the shape of the conversation. The second is the construction of the difficult statement that sits inside it.

Three Beats is the shape. Every human interaction worth having has a beginning, a middle, and an end. The beginning sets context: why are we having this conversation, what is the state of things, what is the agreement we are working from. The middle is where the work gets done: the difficult thing gets said, the issue gets explored, the disagreement gets aired. The end closes: we have decided this, we have agreed to that, we are moving on. Most people who struggle with assertiveness lead with the middle. The difficult statement comes out of nowhere, the room has no context to receive it in, and the conversation collapses into defence and counter-defence. The fix is to do the work the beginning is supposed to do, before you try to do the work the middle is supposed to do.

The Three-Part Assertion (page 17) is the construction. Once you are in the middle of a conversation and you have the context in place, the statement itself has three components: the situation as fact, the feeling owned not weaponised, and the want or need stated specifically. Write it down before you say it. The structure does the work. You do not have to be braver than you are.

Together, the two answer the most common failure mode in this band: the difficult thing delivered without context, without construction, and without a clear close. The room hears a dead cat. With the shape and the construction in place, the room hears a colleague who has thought about this carefully and is doing them the courtesy of saying it plainly.

Speaking up well, again and again, is direct development work. Each conversation handled cleanly updates your sense of yourself as somebody who can be relied on to say the difficult thing. The internal sense follows the external practice.
where_you_might_start: Before any conversation where you know a difficult thing needs to be said, write down the Three Beats. One line each: what is the context, what is the difficult thing, what is the close. The writing is the preparation. The conversation gets dramatically easier once you have done it on paper first.

Use the Three-Part Assertion (page 17) for the difficult statement itself. Situation as fact. Feeling owned, not weaponised. Want or need stated specifically. Optional fourth part: the consequence, stated as information rather than threat. Write it down before you say it. The structure does the work; you do not have to be braver than you are.

When something has been agreed and something else has happened, use the Discrepancy Framework (page 17). Open the conversation on the gap, not on the person. "We agreed X. What I am seeing is Y. Help me understand what has happened." The framework keeps the conversation on the agreement rather than the character of the other person, and tends to produce a useful answer rather than a defensive one.

After any conversation where you said a difficult thing, take five minutes alone to close the loop on the accountability half. Did the thing you said turn out to be right? What happened that you did not predict? What did you learn about how to say it next time? This is the after-action review for assertiveness. Most people do the hard work of speaking up and then never check how it landed. The check is what turns a one-off act of courage into a developing skill.

A3.subtitle: Saying the difficult thing, owning the result, and being specific about what you will do.
A3.next_level_up: Moving up here means saying the thing that needs saying, in the room where it matters, without becoming aggressive or apologetic. You make specific commitments rather than vague ones. You surface disagreement once, briefly, and live with it. The people around you stop having to guess where you stand. They can act on what you said because you said it clearly.
A3.where_it_helps: Where this helps you most: the conversation everyone else is avoiding. You can say the difficult thing in the room, with respect, while it can still be acted on.
A3.where_gain_shows: Where the gain will show first: the point you nearly made. Saying it in the meeting, once, plainly, is usually enough to change what the meeting decides.

A4.name: Growth and Adaptability

strength.what_this_suggests: Your Growth and Adaptability score sits in a strong range. You update your position when shown new evidence. You seek out feedback that is more critical than you are likely to enjoy. You treat unfamiliar situations as material to learn from rather than threats to manage. The visible version of this is someone whose thinking moves forward over time, and whose colleagues can see that movement.
strength.why_it_matters: Adaptability is the behaviour that compounds. Each piece of feedback acted on makes the next one easier to ask for. Each updated position makes the next update more natural. Over a career, the difference between someone who consistently updates and someone who does not is enormous, and most of it is invisible at the level of any single decision.
strength.how_to_use_it_even_better: The development edge for someone with strong adaptability is signal-to-noise. The same openness that lets you update on good evidence can leave you updating on weak evidence too. The skill to develop is filtering: which feedback is from someone whose judgement on this matters, and which is from someone whose comfort you are accidentally optimising for. Adapt to the first. Notice but do not over-weight the second.

development.what_this_score_tells_you:
A note on the concepts before we look at what the score means for you.

Growth and Adaptability are two related skills the questionnaire measures together. Growth, in the charismatic sense, is the willingness to develop. The standing decision that there is more to learn, more to update, and that the current version of you is a work in progress rather than a finished article.

Adaptability is the matching skill on the other side of that willingness: the capacity to actually change your behaviour in response to new information or a new situation. The two need each other. Growth without adaptability produces someone who is genuinely interested in development and somehow keeps doing the same things. Adaptability without growth produces someone who changes shape constantly to fit the room, without ever updating their model of themselves.

Higher scores in this subscale describe someone who updates their position when shown new evidence, who treats unfamiliar situations as material to learn from rather than threats to manage, and who is comfortable being a beginner again in all kinds of situations, because they love to keep on updating themselves. People around them see someone whose thinking develops over time, and respect their flexibility of thought. Lower scores can show up in two distinct ways. The first is the person who is open to feedback in principle but quietly treats their own way of working as the 'right' way; they may even want to grow, but cannot quite bring themselves to change their behaviour. The second is the person who constantly adapts to changing circumstances but never updates the underlying beliefs and principles, so the changes are mostly surface-level and shift back to the old ways if any kind of difficulty is encountered along the way. People around them may see someone who talks a good game about changing, but will soon go back. Read your own profile against the two and decide which is the bigger gap for you.

Now what this score is telling us in your case.

A lower score on this subscale does not usually mean you are resistant to change. Most people in this group believe sincerely in growth and feedback. The gap is more specific. Either the willingness is there and the behavioural change is not: you accept the feedback, agree with the feedback, and then carry on as before, or the change is happening at the surface without touching the deeper habits underneath, so it does not last. Both patterns are signals that updating, as a working skill, is still in progress.
development.what_it_costs_to_leave_this_alone: The cost of staying where you are is slow and invisible. In the short term, nothing dramatic happens. In the longer term, colleagues can change their ways faster than you do, and the gap can widen without anyone mentioning it. The cost to your reputation is that you can become harder to work with as the work itself changes around you, and others tend to notice the drift before you do. The internal cost is harder to spot: you may find yourself describing your weaknesses as fixed features of who you are, rather than things you are working on. The story you tell yourself about yourself becomes the boundary around what you actually try. "I can't change" can get hard-wired into your self-beliefs and painted on the wall for all around you to see.
development.how_to_close_the_gap:
Build two skills, together. The first is the willingness to be a beginner again. The second is the practice of reading the road as you drive.

Most experienced professionals are up to date in the things they have already mastered. Keeping up to date has a cost, but it does not tax you beyond your comfort zone, and because you are already skilled, the learning tends to be easier than starting on something genuinely new. The fix is to take on something at work or at home that is genuinely unfamiliar: a domain you do not yet understand, a tool you have not yet learned, a kind of conversation you have been avoiding, and do it badly for a while. The act of being a beginner again is the strongest single corrective to fixed-feature thinking. You cannot treat your weaknesses as permanent features when you are actively learning something new.

Reading the road is the work for Adaptability. The experienced driver does not wait for the car to spin before adjusting; they read the conditions and adjust the speed and the line before the road forces the change on them. The professional version is the same. When something is not working, the question is not just whether to try harder. The question is whether to try something different or new. Working harder at the same approach is an effort. Working differently is a strategy. Most people in this group default to harder, because harder feels like more effort and therefore more virtue. Differently is where the actual learning is.

Think of this work the way you would think of a physical skill. A Pilates move, a tennis technique. Small changes in technique, with immediate feedback, can make what once seemed impossible immediately feasible. The professional version of that immediate feedback is a trusted colleague whose view you can ask for, regularly. The actions below are designed to give you exactly that: small, specific, with quick feedback built in.

Updating is the work itself. Doing something unfamiliar, and reflecting on what changed, builds your sense of yourself as somebody who can change. The internal version catches up to the external one.
where_you_might_start: In the next month, do something at work or in your personal life that is unfamiliar enough that you are not sure you will be good at it. The act of being a beginner again is the strongest single corrective to fixed-feature thinking. The discomfort is the point. It is what tells you the muscle is working.

When a piece of your work is not working, or when you sense that the way you are doing it is becoming less effective, ask yourself one question before you push harder: am I working harder at this, or am I working differently at this? Both are options. Only one of them is a strategy. The five minutes of reflection before the next attempt is the single highest-return move in this subscale.

Update your thinking. Spend ten minutes reminding yourself of all the times in your life when you have changed your thinking. On relationships, people, technology, politics, whatever it is. Think of what you learned from each specific experience and the process. Are you always right? Does it matter to you to be right? What did you learn about yourself and others when you realised that you were wrong? Then think about a current issue. Is there a chance that you are wrong, or resistant to something now that is affecting your work, life, or happiness? What could you do about that situation? How would it help you, and the people around you?

Get feedback from people you respect, like and trust. Use the Asking For Feedback Worth Getting method from the companion book with one trusted colleague. Specifically ask for the thing that has been uncomfortable to mention. Thank them, write down what they said, and resist the urge to defend or explain in the moment. The next time you ask, the answers will be sharper because the first ask was honoured.

high_band_variant.replace: A lower score on this subscale does not usually mean you are resistant to change. Most people in this group believe sincerely in growth and feedback.
high_band_variant.with: This subscale appears here because it sits below the others in your profile. The score itself is in the higher band, and relative gaps are where the next gains tend to live. Most people at this level believe sincerely in growth and feedback.

A4.subtitle: Updating your position when shown new evidence, and treating feedback as data.
A4.next_level_up: Moving up here means updating well in front of others. You can change your mind about something publicly without it feeling like a defeat. You ask for the feedback that is harder to give. You try things you are not yet good at. The people around you experience someone whose thinking moves forward over time, and they trust you more because of it.
A4.where_it_helps: Where this helps you most: unfamiliar ground. New briefs, new rooms and new evidence read to you as material to learn from, and your thinking visibly moves.
A4.where_gain_shows: Where the gain will show first: the feedback you already collect. Acting on one piece inside a week turns willingness into visible movement.

A5.name: Situational Self-Awareness

strength.what_this_suggests: Your Situational Self-Awareness score sits in a strong range. You can read your own state accurately, in the moment, without performing it and without suppressing it. You can read what a room is carrying, separately from what is on the agenda. The visible version of this is someone whose presence in a meeting is calibrated to what the meeting actually needs, not just to what was planned for it.
strength.why_it_matters: Situational self-awareness is the rarest of the strengths in the model, and the one that quietly underpins all the others. Most people are noticeably worse at this than they think. Eurich's research suggests fewer than fifteen per cent of working adults meet a defensible criterion for being self-aware, even though the great majority believe they are. If you score well here, the people around you experience you as someone who notices things they themselves had not articulated.
strength.how_to_use_it_even_better: The development edge is using this strength to help others develop theirs. People with strong situational awareness are often most useful when they name out loud what they are noticing in the room, not just to act on it themselves. 'It looks like we are pulling in two directions on this, can we name what they are?' is the kind of intervention that only someone reading the room can make. The opportunity is to make those observations available.

development.what_this_score_tells_you:
A note on the concepts before we look at what the score means for you.

Situational Self-Awareness, in the charismatic sense, is the ability to read two things at the same time: your own state in the moment, and the room's reading of you. Both readings have to be reasonably accurate, and the gap between them has to be small enough to correct. Most people in working life are reasonably good at one of the two. Reading your own state, or reading the room. The people at the top of this subscale read both, and notice when their own reading and the room's reading do not match.

The skill is sometimes uncomfortable to develop, because it requires honest engagement with the possibility that the version of you the room is seeing is different from the version you think you are projecting. In some way, closing the gap between what has happened, what it means and what to do about it is a bit like an autopsy. An autopsy is fascinating, until it is you on the table. Most senior professionals are intensely interested in other people's self-awareness gaps. They are far less interested in their own. The work of this subscale is to take the same fascination and turn it inwards.

Higher scores in this subscale describe someone who knows what state they are in before the room does, who reads cues from other people quickly and accurately, and who can adjust in real time when their reading and the room's reading appear to diverge. People around them see the results of those skills. The room reads them as adaptable, attentive to signals, willing to ask, willing to react, and as a result, the people in the room stay engaged, included and respected.

Lower scores can show up in two distinct ways. The first is the person who reads the room well but does not read themselves; they are sensitive to others and sometimes less aware of their own state and impact. The second is the person who reads themselves well, but is sometimes surprised by how the room actually receives them.

Now, what this score is telling us in your case.

A lower score on this subscale does not usually mean you do not pay attention to yourself or to others. Most people in this band pay close attention. The gap is more specific. Either the attention is going to one side of the equation and not the other, or you read both, but do not put the two readings together. The version of you that the room sees, and the version of you that you think you are projecting, are not yet in reliable agreement.
development.what_it_costs_to_leave_this_alone:
The cost of staying where you are is that the room is operating on better information than you are. Other people are reading the gap between your intention and your impact, and they are adjusting their behaviour towards you on the basis of what they see. Over time, they get better at this, and you get no better at all, because nobody tells you about the gap. They simply route around it.

The reputation cost is that you become slightly harder to give feedback to, because the gap keeps appearing, and you keep not noticing it.

The internal cost is harder to spot: the meetings that did not go as you expected, the relationships that have cooled without your understanding why, the patterns of response from others that have shifted without you being able to name what changed. Most of these have answers, and the answers live in the gap you are not yet reading.
development.how_to_close_the_gap:
The skill to build is in play-back and review. Interest in your own reflection, and the careful selection of others whose opinion you respect to ask for feedback. The athlete, with their coach, after a match, watches the footage of their own performance with the same attitude regardless of the result. A win and a loss get the same treatment. The footage shows what the footage shows. What did I do well that is worth keeping? What did I do less well that is worth changing? The result is in the past. The future is the only thing the play-back can affect.

The professional version of the play-back is the same discipline applied to your own working day. At the end of a meeting, a difficult conversation, a presentation, the question is not how did it go. The question is what did I do well that I want to retain, and what could I do differently next time.

Done regularly, the play-back closes the gap between your in-the-moment reading of yourself and the room's reading of you. Done with the same attitude towards wins and losses, it stops the play-back becoming either self-congratulation or self-attack. The footage is just the footage.

The play-back is foundational work. Each piece of accurate self-observation closes the gap between how you read yourself and how the room reads you. That closure is what self-trust is made of.
where_you_might_start: After a meeting or conversation that matters, take three minutes to do a play-back. Two questions only. What did I do well that is worth retaining? What did I do less well that I could do differently next time? Write the answers down. The writing is what turns a feeling into a piece of information you can act on.

Treat wins and losses with the same attention. The temptation after a good event or result is to enjoy it and move on. The temptation after a bad one is to relive it and punish yourself. Both miss the point. The footage from a win and a loss contains the same kind of information, and the work of the play-back is to extract it consistently in both directions.

Once a week, ask someone whose judgement you trust for one specific observation: "When I was [in the meeting / on that call / handling that situation], what do you think I did well and what one thing do you think I could do differently or better next time?" Use the Asking For Feedback Worth Getting method from the companion book. The answer is a piece of footage you could not have shot yourself.

When something the room does surprises you, treat the surprise as data. The surprise is the gap between your reading and theirs. It is the most valuable thing to read in the moment, and the easiest to ignore. Pause. Name what you expected, and what actually happened. The difference is the potential lesson.

A5.subtitle: Reading your own state and the room, in the moment, without performing it or suppressing it.
A5.next_level_up: Moving up here means walking into rooms knowing what version of yourself has arrived, and choosing a different one if the room needs it. You catch your own state before it leaks into your behaviour. You notice what the room is carrying that nobody has named. The people around you experience someone who reads the moment well, and they trust the moments you choose to spend with them more because of it.
A5.where_it_helps: Where this helps you most: the room that has shifted. You read the change while it is happening and adjust before anyone needs to name it.
A5.where_gain_shows: Where the gain will show first: the meetings that currently surprise you. You catch your own state before the room does, and adjust while it still matters.

B1.name: Empathy and Listening

strength.what_this_suggests: Your Empathy and Listening score sits in a strong range. You let people finish before you respond, even when you think you know what to say. You read emotional registers as accurately as verbal content. You adjust your response based on what the other person seems to need, rather than what is convenient to say. The visible version of this is someone other people open up to.
strength.why_it_matters: Listening is the most underestimated of the social skills. People who feel heard tend to think more clearly, decide more cleanly, and trust the relationship more deeply. Over time, the reputation you build as a listener earns you access to information and trust that no other behaviour can.
strength.how_to_use_it_even_better: The development edge here is using this strength in moments that matter, rather than only in moments that are easy. Listening well in a relaxed one-to-one is one thing. Listening well in a meeting where you are under pressure, in a feedback conversation that has tilted, or in a difficult moment with someone you find draining, is a different order of skill. The opportunity is to use it deliberately when the stakes rise rather than letting it default to the easy contexts.

development.what_this_score_tells_you:
A note on the concepts before we look at what the score means for you.

Empathy and Listening are two related skills that the questionnaire measures together. Listening, in the charismatic sense, is the discipline of giving the person in front of you your full attention. Listening as if they were the only thing important to you at that moment. Quietly. Carefully. Actively. Not waiting for your turn to speak. Not running your next sentence in your head while they finish theirs. Not preparing a clever follow-up. Just there, with them, until they have said what they came to say. Until the full-stop appears.

Hearing is the matching skill on the other side of the silence: the capacity to notice what is being (and not being) said underneath the first answer, and to help the person find it and say it. The best friend who knows there is more that has not yet been said, waits long enough for the person to feel the gap for themselves, and sometimes asks the question that helps them go one level deeper. Hearing without listening feels like an inquisition. Listening without hearing produces a sympathetic surface with no substance. The two together produce someone people seek out, and remember, because conversations with them go further than other conversations do.

Higher scores in this subscale describe someone who tends to be fully present with whoever they are speaking to, who notices the gap between the first answer and the full answer, and who creates the space for the second to emerge. People around them often describe the experience of being heard by this person as different from being heard by most others.

Lower scores can show up in two distinct ways. The first is the person who is attentive in the moment but hears only what is being said on the surface: they stay present, but they take the first answer as the answer and often find that they missed the detail later. The second is the person who hears the deeper stuff but cannot stay quiet long enough for the speaker to find them on their own; they ask the right next question too soon, and end up extracting rather than receiving. Read your own profile against the two and decide which is the bigger gap for you.

Now, what this score is telling us in your case.

A lower score on this subscale does not usually mean you do not care about the people you are talking to. Most people in this band care a great deal. The gap is more specific. Either the attention is good, but the depth of listening is shallow, or the hearing is sharp, and the patience is short-lived. Both patterns produce conversations that end one level above where they could have ended. The work is to close that gap.
development.what_it_costs_to_leave_this_alone: The cost is mostly invisible to you, and entirely visible to the people around you. They notice when they have been heard, and they notice when they have not. Over time, people share the parts of themselves and their thinking that the listener has shown they can hold. A listener who only catches the surface gets the surface from then on. A listener who interrupts the depth gets shorter, more guarded answers. The reputational cost is that the people you talk to sometimes leave the conversations with you feeling less heard, loved or respected than they could have been. The internal cost is that you may not know what you are missing, because the depth that you did not reach was the depth you both might have learned most from.
development.how_to_close_the_gap:
The skill to build is two skills, working together. The first is silence with full attention. The second is the patience to let the deeper answer surface in its own time.

Silence with full attention is built by removing the things that compete with it. The internal voice running its next sentence. The instinct to fill any pause that lasts longer than a beat. The half-attention that flickers to the phone, the door, the next meeting. Listening at the charismatic level requires that none of these win. The practice is to notice when they are pulling at you, and to put them down. The effect on the room when you do is large and immediate, and the speaker often notices it before you do.

The patience to let the deeper answer surface is built by trusting that there is one. Most first answers are partial. The speaker is guarded, or simply not ready to share more deeply. They might also be testing whether you are really interested before investing in a deeper conversation. If you fill the silence with your own next question, they might read that as the conversation moving on, and they move on with it. If you wait a beat longer than feels comfortable, with continued full attention, the second answer often arrives on its own. When it does not, the question that helps is rarely clever. It is usually small. "What else?" "Say more about that." "What is underneath that?" The quality of the question matters less than the quality of the attention that comes with it.
where_you_might_start: In your next three meaningful conversations, set yourself one rule: do not speak while the other person is finishing a thought. Even when they pause. Even when you are sure they have finished. Wait a beat longer than feels natural. Most of what you most want to hear arrives in the beat you would normally have filled.

When you do speak in response, default to a next-level question, one that builds on what they have just said, rather than a comment. The comment closes the door; the question keeps it open. Even when you have a clear view of what they should do, hold the view back until they have explored the situation fully in their own words. The view, when it lands, will land better against an understanding the person has helped to build.

Use the Asking For Feedback Worth Getting approach (page 16) with one person you trust. Specific ask: "How can I listen more helpfully to you?" The answer is the diagnostic. Most people who score lower on this subscale are surprised by the answer, and the surprise itself is useful.

Once a week, pick one conversation you had and review it the way an athlete reviews footage. Where did you fill a silence that you could have left? Where did you reply to the surface answer rather than the deeper one? Where did you finish a sentence the other person had not yet finished? The review is the practice. The next conversation gets easier because the last one was looked at.

B1.subtitle: Listening for the full stop rather than the gap, and asking about what was actually said.
B1.next_level_up: Moving up here means people opening up to you more than they used to. You wait until the speaker has actually finished. You ask about something they said rather than about something you were going to say anyway. The people around you start volunteering more of what they actually think, because they trust the listening will be there for it.
B1.where_it_helps: Where this helps you most: the person who has not said the real thing yet. Your listening gives it room to arrive, and people leave your conversations feeling heard.
B1.where_gain_shows: Where the gain will show first: the conversation you would normally steer. Listening past your own next point tends to surface the material the meeting actually needed.

B2.name: Warmth and Social Courtesy

strength.what_this_suggests: Your Warmth and Social Courtesy score sits in a strong range. The pattern this points to is everyday social behaviour that makes people feel welcome and respected. You greet people you do not need anything from. You remember small details and use them lightly. You notice when someone is being left out and include them. You treat junior colleagues with the same courtesy as senior ones.
strength.why_it_matters: Warmth is the texture of how a person occupies shared social space, and it compounds. The cumulative effect of small acts of attention over years is what produces the reputation of being someone other people want to work with. The single warm gesture is not the point. The reliability of warmth across situations is.
strength.how_to_use_it_even_better: The development edge for someone with strong warmth is to keep it visible in the contexts where it matters most. Warmth that everyone receives equally is what builds long-term influence. The risk for high-warmth people is that the warmth is real but selective: a warmer version with familiar people, a more functional version with everyone else. The opportunity is to notice that gap and close it deliberately.

development.what_this_score_tells_you:
A note on the concepts before we look at what the score means for you.

Warmth and Social Courtesy, in the charismatic sense, describes the quality of attention you give to another person, combined with the willingness to ask more of them when that serves them. Generous attention is the foundation: the small repeated acts of consideration, the eye contact that lasts, the question that shows you remember what they told you last time, the compliment given because you noticed something worth noticing. Social courtesy is the same thing expressed at scale, across the dozens of small interactions that make up a working day. The willingness to ask more is what stops warmth from decaying into pure niceness. Warmth that never challenges, never expects, never holds the other person to anything, eventually shrinks to flattery. The two together are what make warmth substantial.

Higher scores in this subscale describe the kind of person you might remember from your own experience, because they showed you they cared about you while demanding more of you. Their challenge and support was always for your benefit, not theirs. The teacher who pushed you when you were ready to coast. The boss who told you the truth at the moment you most needed to hear it. The friend who took you seriously enough to point at the thing you were avoiding. People who experience this kind of tough love tend to develop in response to it, and they tend to seek it out for the rest of their lives.

Lower scores in this subscale rarely mean coldness. Most people in this band are perfectly capable of warmth and do not withhold it on purpose. The gap is more specific. The most common pattern is the compliment that comes with a catch: warmth that is real in the moment, but that turns out to be a setup for an ask, a softener for bad news, or a deposit being made against a withdrawal that comes later. The other common pattern is warmth that is genuine but undemanding. The person is well-liked, but the relationships they build do not produce growth in the other person, because nothing is ever asked of the other person beyond compliance with the relationship itself.

Now, what this score is telling us in your case.

The diagnostic line is simple. Did the compliment come with a catch? Or was it just a compliment? The catch can be small. A compliment followed by "and one small thing..." A piece of recognition that ends with a request. A piece of warmth that arrives shortly before the difficult conversation. Most people who score lower on this subscale are not being insincere. They are bundling warmth with utility, and the people they are warm to can often tell. The most valuable work here is to unbundle the two.
development.what_it_costs_to_leave_this_alone: Conditional warmth corrodes relationships slowly, in a way that is hard to spot from the inside. The people on the receiving end learn, over time, to brace slightly when they are about to be complimented, because the compliment is often the lead-up to something else. They cannot always name what they are bracing against, but the bracing is real, and it costs you the easy access to them that pure warmth would have bought. Over a working life, the cumulative cost is significant. The relationships that should be your strongest become the relationships that are most carefully managed. You may end up working harder than your peers to get the same response from people, because the people are slightly more guarded with you than they would be with somebody whose warmth carries no charge.
development.how_to_close_the_gap:
The skill to build is the no-catch praise or compliment. The compliment, the question, the piece of attention, the small kindness, given without any of it being attached to something you want from the person. Most people in this band are perfectly capable of generous attention. The work is to keep it generous when there is also something you want. The fix is to separate the two. Give the warmth in one moment, with nothing attached. Make the ask in a separate moment, on its own terms. The relationship gets stronger because the warmth has been established, and the ask gets a better answer because the asker is trusted.

The second half of the work, once the no-catch discipline is in place, is the willingness to add the challenge part. Warmth that never asks anything of the other person is comfortable to give and comfortable to receive, but it does not develop either of you. The teacher you remember who pushed you outside your comfort zone. The boss you most respect told you an uncomfortable truth. The friend you most trust who holds you to a higher standard than you sometimes hold yourself to. Once you are sure that your generosity is reliably unconditional, the challenge becomes more effective, because the other person knows the challenge is not a catch.
where_you_might_start: For one week, give a piece of unprompted warmth to one person each day, with no ask attached. A specific compliment about something you have noticed. A thank you for something they did that you have not mentioned before. A question about how a thing they were working on turned out. No follow-up request. No hidden purpose. The discipline is to give warmth and let it stand.

The next time you are about to compliment someone shortly before asking something of them, separate the two. Give the compliment now. Make the ask tomorrow, or in a separate conversation. Most lower-B2 patterns are this exact pattern repeated many times. Breaking the bundle, even once, changes how the person on the receiving end experiences the warmth.

For one relationship where the warmth is reliable, add one piece of honest challenge. The kind of thing you would say to the friend you most respect. Something the person needs to hear, said with care, framed as a sign of how much you take them seriously. If the warmth has been unconditional up to that point, the challenge lands as a deepening of the relationship rather than a threat to it.

Use the Asking For Feedback Worth Getting method from the companion book with one person you have known for a long time. Specific ask: "Am I conditional or unconditional in my use of warmth or praise?" The answer is the diagnostic. Most people who score lower on this subscale are surprised by where the catches have landed, and the specifics are what the development work is.

B2.subtitle: Everyday warmth that does not depend on what the other person can do for you.
B2.next_level_up: Moving up here means people feel acknowledged in your presence, regardless of their position relative to yours. You greet, you remember, you follow up. The pattern of small attentions is reliable. The people around you, including the ones who do not benefit you directly, speak well of you when you are not in the room. That is the quiet long-term effect.
B2.where_it_helps: Where this helps you most: first meetings, cold starts, and the conversations nobody else wants to open. The room you walk into tends to relax.
B2.where_gain_shows: Where the gain will show first: the people at the edge of your working day. Small, reliable courtesy with them builds a reputation the centre cannot build on its own.

B3.name: Conversational Skills

strength.what_this_suggests: Your Conversational Skills score sits in a strong range. You ask questions that move the conversation forward, rather than questions that perform interest. You yield the floor without losing the thread. You end conversations cleanly. You adapt your register to the person you are with.
strength.why_it_matters: Conversational skill is the mechanical side of social effectiveness, and it is what makes the difference between someone who can be effective in a familiar setting and someone who can land in any setting. Strong conversational craft is what lets warmth and empathy actually arrive in the room, rather than being held back by clunky turn-taking or mis-pitched register.
strength.how_to_use_it_even_better: The development edge is the conversation that gets to the second level. Most conversations stay at the polite-exchange surface. The skill to develop is moving them, gently, to the layer underneath: the specific worry, the half-mentioned detail, the thing the speaker almost said and chose not to. The strokes-and-clicks practice in the companion book sets out how. People who can find the second layer reliably are rare.

development.what_this_score_tells_you:
A note on the concepts before we look at what the score means for you.

Conversational Skills, in the charismatic sense, describes the rhythm-keeping work that lets a conversation be a real conversation rather than two people taking turns to wait. Think of it as the work of the drummer in the band. The drummer is not the showy member. The drummer is the one who provides the beat that allows everybody else to express themselves in unison. Without the drummer, the band collapses into parallel solos. With the drummer, the music has shape, the players know when to come in, and the room hears something larger than the sum of the players.

In building your conversational skills to expert level, this means allowing the people you meet to speak first and more than you. They hold centre stage, and you are there to make them look, sound and feel good. Here is the detail:

Initiating conversation. Starting the conversation in a way that makes it easy for the other person to speak. The opening question, general and non-intrusive, followed by another easy question: the "how are you" opener, followed by "how did the meeting go this morning", and then clicking (like a hyperlink on a website) on whatever they say to go one level deeper. The opening is reinforced by stroking: the small physical, audible, verbal and non-verbal signals that tell the speaker you are with them and want them to continue. Stroking and clicking, as the book describes them, are the two techniques that turn co-presence into actual conversation.

Reading the rhythm. Knowing when to throw and when to catch. When the room needs more energy from you, and when it needs less. Picking up the tempo of the moment.

Including others. Making sure everyone in the conversation has space to contribute, especially the quieter person, the newer person, the one being slightly talked over. The conversational skill is the small move that says, "I think Sarah has been waiting to say something on this," or "What do you make of it, Tom?" These moves cost the person making them almost nothing, and change the experience of the conversation for everyone in the room.

Holding the structure. Knowing where the conversation is going, when it has drifted, when it needs to land. Bringing it back when it wanders. Closing when it is time to close. The small move that says, "Coming back to the question we started with..." or "If we are going to make a decision today, what do we need to agree?"

The four together produce the drummer effect. The conversation has shape. Everybody gets to play. The room sounds better than it would have without your skills.

Higher scores in this subscale describe someone who is the rhythm section in most conversations they are part of, often without anyone noticing they are doing it. People around them have the experience of conversations that go further, include more people, and end somewhere useful. Lower scores can show up in different ways depending on which facet of the rhythm work has not yet developed: the person who initiates well but cannot read when their lead is over; the person who reads rhythm but never initiates; the person who includes everyone but has no view of their own; the person so focused on structure that the conversation never breathes. Read your own profile against the four and notice which is the bigger gap for you.

Now, what this score is telling us in your case.

A lower score on this subscale rarely means you are bad at conversations. Most people in this band are perfectly capable of a good conversation when the conditions are right. The gap is more specific. One of the four facets of the work has not yet developed at the same level as the others, and the conversations you are in might suffer for it in a way that is hard to spot without the diagnostic. The work is to identify the specific facet and develop it directly.
development.what_it_costs_to_leave_this_alone: Most of the cost is invisible to the people who carry it, which is part of why it can persist for years. Conversations that should go further end at the surface. Meetings you were part of produce decisions that ignore something you had a view on, because the rhythm of the room did not let your view land. Less confident and expressive people in your conversations might stay quieter than they would otherwise have done, because the conversation did not include them. Over time, the conversations you are part of might be less productive, less inclusive, and less memorable than they could have been. Imagine the sense of pride in a colleague who has been asked for their opinion and listened to in a room full of senior managers. The reputation cost is small per conversation and large per career, because conversational skills are one of the most visible skills a person has, even when it is invisible to the person doing it.
development.how_to_close_the_gap:
The skill to build is the skill in the specific facet that is your gap. Each facet has its own practice.

If initiating is the gap, the work is to practise the layered opening. The easy first question. The easy second question that earns the right to the slightly deeper one. The small encouragements that keep the other person going. Most people in this band can do this, but do it inconsistently. The work is to make it the default opening for any conversation that matters.

If reading the rhythm is the gap, the work is to notice the room's tempo before you contribute. A short pause before you speak, in which you ask yourself a single question: does this room need me to throw, or to catch? Throwing is offering something: a question, a view, an observation. Catching is receiving what is being offered. Both are useful; both are needed. The rhythm work is choosing the right one for the moment.

If including others is the gap, the work is to keep one eye on the people who have not yet spoken. Once per conversation, deliberately, make the move that invites somebody else in. The cost to you is small. The effect on the room is big, because the people who have been included tend to remember it for longer than the people who included them.

If holding the structure is the gap, the work is the small move that brings the conversation back to its purpose. "We started this conversation talking about X. Where have we got to?" "If we are going to agree on something today, what is the something?" These are the skills that keep the conversation from drifting past the point where it could have landed.
where_you_might_start: For one week, open every meaningful conversation with the layered opening. The easy first question. The easy second question. The small encouragements that keep the person going. Notice how often the second question earns access to a piece of information you would not otherwise have heard. The pattern is the practice.

Once per day, in a conversation that matters, ask yourself the throw-or- catch question before you speak. Just once per day to start. The pause is small. The effect on what you choose to say is large.

In one meeting this week where there is a junior or quieter person, deliberately make one move to include them. "What do you think, X?" The move costs almost nothing. It also signals to the rest of the room how you treat the people whose voices are harder to hear.

Use the Asking For Feedback Worth Getting method from the companion book with one colleague who is in many of the same conversations as you. Specific ask: "In our meetings, what would you like more of from me: better starts, better reading of the room, more inclusion of others, or sharper closes?" The answer is the diagnostic, and the specific facet is the development work.

B3.subtitle: Asking questions that move the conversation forward, and ending it cleanly.
B3.next_level_up: Moving up here means your conversations land somewhere rather than just running. You ask about the thing they actually said, not the thing you came in with. You yield the floor without losing the thread. You finish conversations cleanly. The people around you describe time with you as worth their while, rather than something they got through.
B3.where_it_helps: Where this helps you most: rooms where the agenda is loose and the stakes are personal. You can take a conversation to the second layer, where the useful material lives.
B3.where_gain_shows: Where the gain will show first: the conversations that currently stall. One better question, and the willingness to wait for the answer, moves them somewhere useful.

B4.name: Emotional Control and Humility

strength.what_this_suggests: Your Emotional Control and Humility score sits in a strong range. You stay steady when contradicted in front of others. You give credit specifically and publicly. You can say 'I do not know' without self-deprecation. You do not need to be the smartest voice in the conversation.
strength.why_it_matters: Emotional control and humility together produce a particular kind of credibility. The people around you trust that they will not be embarrassed by you, that the praise will be shared accurately, and that what you do not know will be admitted rather than disguised. This is the foundation of long-term professional trust.
strength.how_to_use_it_even_better: The development edge is to make these behaviours visible in the moments they cost something. Sharing credit when the credit is small is one thing. Sharing credit when the credit is large, and you could plausibly have kept it, is what builds reputation. Admitting you do not know in a low-stakes meeting is one thing. Admitting it in a high-stakes one is what builds trust. The opportunity is to use these moves where the cost is real and the effect is largest.

development.what_this_score_tells_you:
A note on the concepts before we look at what the score means for you.

Emotional Control and Humility are two related skills that the questionnaire measures together. Emotional Control, in the charismatic sense, is the ability to manage your own state so that you do not amplify whatever is difficult in the room. The calmest person in the room, who would never leap to conclusions even if the building was on fire. Their presence reduces the temperature when things get hard, not because they feel nothing, but because they choose to feel it without making the room about their reaction to it.

Humility is the matching skill on the other side: the willingness not to centre yourself in the room when you could. The senior person who is there to serve the room or the event, whatever their seniority and whatever their role. They take the role the room most needs. They might even be invisible until they step in to help. The two together produce a person whose presence the room benefits from, without anybody having to comment on the presence directly. The room is calmer and more inclusive when they are in it.

Higher scores in this subscale describe someone who manages their state in real time and sets their status aside when the room needs something other than status. People around them notice the effect more than the person. Difficult meetings become more workable. Quieter voices get heard. The room ends up somewhere it could not have got to without the high-B4 person, and nobody mentions them by name in the debrief.

Lower scores can show up in four distinct patterns, two for each skill.

For Emotional Control, the first pattern is the person who amplifies. When something goes wrong, the room becomes about their reaction to the wrongness. The visible feeling becomes the new problem the room has to handle. The second pattern is the person who suppresses.
