The control looks total from the outside, but it costs the person a great deal to hold, and tends to leak at the seams in ways the room can sense: the tight tone, the clipped reply, the held-back comment that comes out three meetings later.

For Humility, the first pattern is the person who centres themselves. The room needs to acknowledge their expertise, their status, or their experience before it can proceed. The second pattern is the person pretending to be humble. The false modesty, the "I am just here to learn" line from somebody who is clearly there to lead. Both centring and pretended humility cost the room something the room could have used.

Read your own profile against the four and notice which is the bigger gap for you.

Now, what this score is telling us in your case.

A lower score on this subscale rarely means you have no control over yourself or that you think too highly of yourself. Most people in this band have plenty of self-control and a balanced view of their own importance. The gap is more specific. Either your state management is not yet reliable under pressure, or your status is showing in places the room would rather not have to manage. Both patterns are normal, and both are addressable. The work is to identify which one is yours and develop the specific practice.
development.what_it_costs_to_leave_this_alone:
Over time, the people you work with might quietly start managing meetings to avoid the conditions that trigger your less helpful reactions. The conversations you most need to be part of might happen without you, because including you could add an extra variable to a meeting that was already complex.

People who struggle to regulate their emotions, whatever they do, can appear inconsistent to others. So other people can become unsure which version of you they are going to get in any given moment, and adjust their opinion of you accordingly.

For leaders, this can mean that their experience of other people narrows. Meetings can become more about your state than about the meeting itself. Other people contribute less, because the cost of speaking up in your presence might seem higher than the cost of staying quiet. Over time, you might lose access to the views you most need, because the people who hold them have learned not to share them.

The cost of fake humility is the most subtle of the four. The room can usually tell. The performance of humility can read like a small piece of dishonesty, and over time, cost trust. Even when the room cannot name what is wrong, the person pretending to be humble tends to be slightly less trusted than the one being truthfully important.
development.how_to_close_the_gap:
The skill to build is state management, or a service-mentality, or both. They respond to different work.

State management is built by noticing your own state before the room does. The discipline is to put a beat between the trigger and the response. The calmest person in the room is not the person who feels nothing. They are the person who has trained the gap between feeling and reacting to be long enough that the reaction can be chosen. The skill is short, repeated, and gets easier with practice. The room sees the gap as composure, and the composure does the work that amplifying or suppressing would have undermined.

Service mentality is built by asking a question before you enter the room. What does the room most need from me today? Is it leading? Is it asking the question that gives somebody else room to lead? Is it protecting space for a quieter person to speak? Is it taking the notes? The question commits you to a role rather than a status. The role might match your title; it might not. Either way, the room benefits, and the practice over time produces the kind of person other people quietly seek out.
where_you_might_start: The next time you feel a piece of difficulty starting to rise in a meeting: frustration, irritation, the urge to react. Give yourself one beat before you respond. Just one. The beat is the gap. The reaction after the beat is almost always more useful than the one that would have arrived without it.

Before your next important meeting, ask yourself one question: what does this room most need from me today? Decide on the role before you arrive. The role might be nothing to do with the one your title implies. The room will benefit, and the practice will start.

In a meeting where you would normally contribute early, hold the contribution back until at least three other people have spoken. Notice what the room does in the space you would have filled. Notice what gets said that would not have been said if you had spoken first.

Use the Asking For Feedback Worth Getting method from the companion book with one colleague who has seen you in several pressured situations. Specific ask: "How can I be more helpful to others in the meetings I am in? How can I be of more service to this meeting?" The answers are the diagnostic, and the specific fixes are your development work.

B4.subtitle: Choosing what emotional output goes into the room, and sharing credit without performance.
B4.next_level_up: Moving up here means staying steady when contradicted, naming what other people contributed when you are praised, and saying you do not know without self-deprecation. You are not the loudest voice. The people around you trust that they will not be embarrassed by you, that credit will be shared accurately, and that what you do not know will be admitted. That trust takes years to build and minutes to lose.
B4.where_it_helps: Where this helps you most: provocation. When someone pushes, you stay on the subject and let the slight pass, and the room trusts you more for it.
B4.where_gain_shows: Where the gain will show first: the moment you feel the heat rise. A beat of control there protects the relationship and keeps the decision on its merits.

B5.name: Authentic vs Performed Social Behaviour

strength.what_this_suggests: Your Authentic vs Performed score sits in a strong range. The pattern this points to is consistency of social skill across audiences. The same quality of attention shows up for the most junior person in the meeting and the most senior. The same warmth shows up regardless of what the other person can do for you. The volume changes. The vocabulary changes. The amount you reveal changes. What does not change is who you are underneath the adjustments.
strength.why_it_matters: Consistency across audiences is the rarest of the social skills in the model, and the most diagnostic of long-term influence. People who are visibly the same person regardless of who is in the room become the people other people trust most. The opposite pattern, where warmth varies by stakes, is felt by the people on the receiving end even when they cannot name it. They simply find themselves trusting that person less over time.
strength.how_to_use_it_even_better: The development edge is to be deliberate about where this strength is visible. The very people who score well here often have it taken for granted. Make it visible in moments where others would not bother: the conversation with the temp, the follow-up with someone you will not see again, the genuine engagement with the person whose name nobody else remembers. Those are the moments that build long-term reputation.

development.what_this_score_tells_you:
A note on the concepts before we look at what the score means for you.

Authentic Social Behaviour, in the charismatic sense, describes whether your warmth, courtesy, attention and interest are coming from a real underlying disposition or being used deliberately as a tool. The behaviours themselves can look identical from the outside. The difference is what is underneath them. Authentic warmth is the warmth you actually have, showing up in the room. Performed warmth is the same behaviour, put on for the situation, without the underlying feeling that would normally produce it.

This subscale is related to the Charismatic Consistency Index, but it measures something different. The Index reads whether your warmth shows up reliably across the audiences in your life. This subscale reads whether the warmth itself is real when it appears. The two questions are independent. A person can show warmth reliably across audiences and still be performing it. That can be a useful tool for the occasions when you are not feeling it and want to maintain your energy. A person who can show genuine warmth, but who only finds it for certain audiences, is limited by this lack. And a person who can find it even when they are not feeling it can have more impact when they need it most. Both readings tell you something the other cannot see.

Higher scores in this subscale describe someone who turns up the same in every room they enter. The warmth they show their oldest friend is recognisably the same warmth they show a new junior colleague. Not identical in tone or volume, but the same in kind. People around them have the experience of meeting one person rather than a series of polished versions of one person, and they tend to trust that person more deeply over time, because the person has been the same person each time.

Lower scores can show up in two distinct patterns. The first is the deliberate performer. The person who knows what social skills look like and uses them strategically, with the calculation slightly visible to the people on the receiving end. The second is the unconscious performer. The warmth has become a habit, but is not connected to genuine feeling. The behaviours still arrive on time, in the right place, but they are automatic and can seem slightly hollow.

The deliberate performer can stop performing if they choose to. The unconscious performer often does not know they are doing it and is less effective as a result.

Note: we are not saying that authenticity is always a good thing. There are few more irritating people in the world than those whose "authenticity" is unmoderated, or uncontrolled. They can appear vain, self-interested and lacking in social courtesy. Read your own profile against the two patterns and notice which is the most like you and where the most help lies for you to develop.

Now, what this score is telling us in your case.

A lower score on this subscale rarely means that you are insincere. Most people in this band are sincere about wanting to connect with others, and the behaviours they are showing are not chosen to manipulate. The gap is between the behaviour and the feeling underneath it. Either the calculation is showing more than the reader thinks, or the connection between the act and the feeling has thinned over time without the reader noticing. The work is to close the gap between what you are doing and what you actually feel.
development.what_it_costs_to_leave_this_alone:
People can usually tell the difference between somebody who wants something from them and somebody who is glad they are in the room. They cannot always name what they are feeling, but they see it. The cost is that trust can narrow when people feel like they are being deceived, even in small ways. Friends and colleagues of the unaware pretender may still like the person, and may still work with them productively, but their trust usually only extends a certain way, because the person they have met has not been consistent in their behaviour.

Over the longer term, the cost might show up in the kinds of relationships that only develop when both people have shown each other the same version of themselves consistently. These are the relationships that produce the opportunities, the introductions, the openness, the protection in difficult moments. They are also the relationships that make the work feel like work worth doing. Inauthentic behaviour over time tends to produce transactional relationships.
development.how_to_close_the_gap:
The skill to build is in reconnecting the behaviour to the feeling. Not dropping the social skills: they are still useful, and the practised version of warmth is often better than the unpractised version. The work is to make sure the warmth you are showing is the warmth you actually have.

The practice has two parts. The first is noticing, in the moment, when the behaviour and the feeling are out of step. The smile you are about to produce. The question you are about to ask. The piece of advice or help or praise that you are about to share. Pause for a beat. Is the underlying feeling there? If it is, it will land better for the pause, because it will land with sincerity behind it. If it is not, the pause is the moment to either find the feeling or skip the behaviour. The smile that does not land is worse than no smile. The question asked without genuine interest is often worse than no question.

The second part of the practice is harder. Where the feeling is reliably absent, ask why. Is it that the person in front of you does not actually matter to you, and the warmth has been a way of behaving as if they did? Is it that the role you are playing in the room requires warmth, and you have not yet found the version of it that is yours? Is it that you used to feel it and have stopped, and the behaviour has continued out of habit? Each answer points to a different piece of work. None of them is fixed by performing more convincingly. Most of them are fixed by addressing what is underneath.
where_you_might_start: For one week, when you are about to do something that is part of the routine: the ritualised kindness, the morning greeting, the corridor smile, the quick question about the weekend. Pause for one beat and check whether the feeling is there. If it is, say it, do it, and let it land. If it is not, notice the absence and let the moment pass without the performance. The notice itself is the practice.

Pick three people you regularly interact with whom you find yourself performing for. For each, ask one question of yourself: what are the positive things about this person that I have not noticed in a while? Find one specific thing. Something they did well, something about their situation, something you genuinely respect or like. The answer to the question is the way back to the feeling.

The next time you are about to ask a follow-up question of someone, check whether you actually want to know the answer. If you do, ask it. If you do not, do not ask it. The unwanted follow-up question is one of the most common signals of fake warmth, and the easiest one to stop.

Use the Asking For Feedback Worth Getting method from the companion book with one person who has known you a long time and will be honest. Specific ask: "When do you experience me at my best and most sincere?" The honest answer is the most accurate diagnostic in the report, and the patterns the answer points at are the development work.

B5.subtitle: The same person turning up across audiences. Surface adapts. Principle holds.
B5.next_level_up: Moving up here means people on the periphery of your orbit experiencing the same standard of warmth and attention as the people at the centre. The volume changes. The vocabulary changes. The amount you reveal changes. What does not change is who you are underneath the adjustments. The people around you, all of them, speak about you in similar terms.
B5.where_it_helps: Where this helps you most: long relationships and repeat rooms. People test consistency over time, and yours holds, which is what turns liking into trust.
B5.where_gain_shows: Where the gain will show first: the audiences that get the functional version of you. Bringing the same warmth there widens your reach at very low cost.

methods._meta: Half-page summaries of the seventeen named methods from the OSCI Pro Practice Content Library. The report includes three to five of these per respondent, chosen by relevance to their priority subscales.

M1.name: The three-part assertion statement
M1.summary: The structured way to say a difficult thing without it becoming aggressive or apologetic. Three parts: the situation as fact ('I have been waiting three days, and you said I would have it today'), your feelings owned not weaponised ('I feel let down because I believed what you said'), and your want or need stated specifically ('I need your decision now'). An optional fourth part is the 'or else': not a threat, but information that helps the other person make an informed choice. Write it down before you say it. The structure does the work; you do not have to be braver than you are.

M2.name: The discrepancy framework
M2.summary: Used when something has been agreed and something else has happened. Opens the conversation on the gap, not on the person. The structure is short: 'We agreed X. What I am seeing is Y. Help me understand what has happened.' The framework keeps you on the gap rather than on the character of the other person, which tends to produce a useful answer rather than a defensive one.

M3.name: Giving feedback that lands
M3.summary: Three components: specific behaviour observed ('In the meeting on Tuesday, when X raised the budget question, you cut across her'), specific impact ('She did not raise it again, and we left without an answer'), and a clear ask for next time ('Could you let her finish even when you disagree?'). Feedback that lands is feedback that names a behaviour, names an impact, and names an alternative. Anything less specific tends to be heard as a personal criticism and resisted accordingly.

M4.name: Asking for feedback worth getting
M4.summary: Vague asks ('any feedback for me?') get vague answers. The structured ask gets useful ones. Try: 'What one thing could I do differently to be more effective for you?' Or: 'If you had to describe how I work in three words, what would you say?' Or: 'When have I been at my best with you, and when have I been at my worst?' The specificity in the question is what produces specificity in the answer.

M5.name: The five-minutes practice
M5.summary: Before any meeting that matters, take five minutes for four short steps. Name what you are carrying: tiredness, residue from the last interaction, anxiety about a different problem. Imagine what the room might need from this meeting that they may not have said. Choose the state you are going to bring: which version of you is going to be useful here. Reset the body: water, breath, posture. The practice is short. The effect is the gap between an interaction that drifts and one that lands.

M6.name: Reading the room before you walk into it
M6.summary: Most meetings are walked into without preparation, and the cost is paid in the first five minutes when you are still working out what the room is carrying. The check-in: before the meeting, ask one person already in it what the state of things is. The pre-meeting note: write one sentence on what the meeting needs from you that may not be on the agenda. The expectation set: be clear with yourself, before you walk in, on what you want to leave the room with. None of these takes more than a few minutes. All of them compound.

M7.name: Surface adapts, principle holds
M7.summary: The volume changes. The vocabulary changes. The amount you reveal changes. The standard of warmth, attention, and courtesy you bring does not. This is the operational discipline of authentic social behaviour, and it answers the most common misunderstanding about consistency. Consistency does not mean being the same across audiences. It means the principle underneath your behaviour stays steady, even where the surface adapts appropriately to the situation.

M8.name: In good faith with yourself
M8.summary: The word confidence comes from the Latin 'con fides', meaning in good faith. The actor's version: you cannot perform confidence without being in good faith with yourself first. Three layers: self-esteem (in good faith with who you are), self-confidence (in good faith with what you can do), and external confidence (in good faith with the room). The work is not on the external layer. It is on the two underneath, which produce the external layer as a by-product.

M9.name: The car-not-starting principle
M9.summary: When something goes wrong, treat it the way you would treat your car not starting. Diagnose the actual problem. Get help if you need it. Fix the specific thing. Learn from it. Move on. Personal verdicts about your competence are not part of the protocol. The same posture applies to a meeting that did not go well, a piece of work that came back with criticism, or a relationship that has gone cold. The diagnostic, fix, learn, move-on sequence is short, specific, and does not collapse into character judgements.

M10.name: Composure under load
M10.summary: Composure is not stoicism. It is staying functional while you feel what you feel. Three components: slow down by one beat before you respond, name your state to yourself before it leaks into your behaviour, and ask what the next useful action is rather than what the most justified reaction would be. Composure is not the absence of feeling. It is the discipline of choosing what to put into the room while the feeling is doing its work elsewhere.

M11.name: Three principles for handling pressure
M11.summary: Most professional pressure is not the kind of pressure your brain is treating it as. Three principles for putting it in perspective. One: nobody cares as much as you think. The room is not paying as much attention to your performance as you are. Two: nobody is going to die. The catastrophic framing is rarely accurate. Three: get over yourself. Self-consciousness is attention pointed in the wrong direction; redirecting it outward dissolves most of the pressure.

M12.name: Updating well
M12.summary: Updating a position out loud is one of the strongest signals of professional credibility. The structure: 'I had thought X. Having heard Y, I now think Z.' Three sentences. The act of updating publicly normalises updating for you and for everyone watching. People who never update look certain in the moment but lose credibility over time. People who update well look open in the moment and gain credibility over time.

M13.name: The fascinated listener
M13.summary: Two operational components. One: listen for the full stop, not the gap. Wait until the speaker actually has nothing more to say. The full stop is felt by the other person as respect. Two: notice the hyperlinks in what people say. The specific phrases, named worries, half-mentioned details. Each is a door to the next level of the speaker's thinking. The follow-up question is the click.

M14.name: Conditional and unconditional warmth
M14.summary: Conditional warmth is what most adults default to: warm with people who matter to them, functional with people who do not. Unconditional warmth is what people remember: the same standard of attention regardless of audience. The Matt and Stan illustration in the book makes the contrast vivid. The cost of conditional warmth is asymmetric and slow. The benefit of unconditional warmth compounds over years.

M15.name: Strokes and clicks
M15.summary: A stroke is a deliberate act of attention to the other person: noticing what they said, asking about it specifically, returning to it later. A click is the moment they open up because the stroke landed. Four stages: stimulus, response, reward, repeat. The method is taken from Eric Berne's Transactional Analysis and adapted for conversational practice. Three failure modes: manufactured strokes (felt as fake), clicking too fast (felt as pressure), preparing the next question while the answer is still being given (felt as inattention).

M16.name: The five layers of conversation
M16.summary: Adapted from Perls's five layers of neurosis. Most conversations stay at the surface: cliché, role, impasse. The deeper layers are honest version and breakthrough, and they are accessed by the right kind of question. The most useful single move is the shift from 'why' to 'how'. 'Why' asks the speaker to justify, which tends to pull them back to the role layer. 'How' asks them to describe or stay with what is happening, which lets them go further down.

M17.name: The room does not need you to be the loudest
M17.summary: Composure in disagreement, specific credit-sharing, and saying 'I do not know' without self-deprecation, all together. The discipline is letting the room not need you to be the loudest. The cost of being the loudest is that people stop bringing their best thinking to you. The benefit of letting the room have its own voice is that the room thinks more clearly and you get the credit for the conditions rather than the volume.

headline_prompt_template:
You are writing the single-sentence headline for the cover of an OSCI Pro charisma development report.

# The respondent's scores

Quadrant: {quadrant_label} ({quadrant_tagline})
Confidence: {confidence}/100, band: {confidence_band}
Social Skills: {social_skills}/100, band: {social_skills_band}
Charismatic Consistency Index: {consistency_index}/100, band: {consistency_band}

Two lowest subscales (development priorities):
- {priority_1_code} {priority_1_name}: {priority_1_score}/100 ({priority_1_band})
- {priority_2_code} {priority_2_name}: {priority_2_score}/100 ({priority_2_band})

Two highest subscales (strengths):
- {strength_1_code} {strength_1_name}: {strength_1_score}/100
- {strength_2_code} {strength_2_name}: {strength_2_score}/100

# The task

Write the headline. One short sentence, or two short sentences. No more. The reader sees it on the cover. They must read it in a breath.

The headline should:
- name what is already working as the starting point
- gesture at the development area as the opportunity, not the gap
- end on the move that is available

One hard constraint above every style rule: never praise a skill measured by either development priority listed above ({priority_1_code} {priority_1_name} and {priority_2_code} {priority_2_name}). Praise comes only from the two strength subscales. The cover must not contradict the report that follows it.

# The voice

The OSCI Pro report follows a strict voice. The principles below catch the most common failure modes. Follow all of them.

1. Opportunity framing, not deficit framing. Name what the reader has and where the next move is, not what they lack. "The work is widening the reach" not "the gap is reach". Never name a band, score, or pattern as a deficit, weakness, or problem.

2. Plain register. UK English. Short words. Cut every word that does not earn its place. "Use" not "leverage". "Read" not "discern". "Now" not "at this juncture".

3. No antithesis. Antithesis is defining something by first stating what it is NOT. ALL of these forms are banned, not only the first: "not just X but Y"; "not X, but Y"; "X rather than Y" used to define; "less about X than about Y"; "not only X but also Y"; and the split form "It is not about X. It is about Y." THE TEST: if a line reaches its point by first telling the reader what the thing is not, delete the negative half and state what it IS. "steady rather than effusive" becomes "a steady, reliable presence".

4. No clichés or pop-business idioms. No "unlock", "land", "show up", "shows up", "earned the right to be in the room", "where your real charisma lives", "the next chapter", "growth journey", "moving the needle".

5. No "version of you" or "the real you" language. The construct is consistency, not authenticity. The reader is one person whose warmth and attention may reach further or less far.

6. Describe by effect on others, not internal state of the reader. "People in the room hear what you mean" not "you communicate clearly". The instrument measures patterns visible from outside.

7. No em dashes. No contractions ("you are" not "you're"). No exclamation marks. No questions to the reader.

8. Specific over elegant. "Read the room well" not "have strong situational intelligence". Use a concrete word over a generalising one wherever possible.

9. The reader is a senior professional. Write at the level of a thoughtful friend, not a coach or a consultant. No therapy language. No coaching language.

10. When the report makes a claim about itself, frame from the reader's perspective. "The work this report sets out" not "the framework this report provides".

# Good examples (write at this level)

"You read the room well. The next move is widening that to people on the periphery as well as those who matter most."
"The presence is already there. The work is making it as available on the average day as on the best one."
"You listen better than most people in your line of work. The opportunity is using that strength deliberately when the stakes are highest."
"Competent and connected. The work is consistency."
"Connects naturally. The next move is claiming the space that matches the contribution."

These examples show register and length. Do not reuse their content: before borrowing any named skill, check it against the two development priorities above. If reading the room is a priority, the headline must not say the reader reads the room well.

# Bad examples (do not write like this)

"You have the confidence and adaptability to lead well. The work now is steadying yourself under pressure so that strength shows up just as clearly in difficult moments as it does in calm ones." (too long, antithesis, "shows up", consultant register)
"You leverage strong stakeholder management capabilities while exhibiting opportunities for growth in behavioural consistency." (jargon)
"Your weakness is consistency." (deficit-framed, bare)
"You're not just an empathic listener, you're a charismatic leader." (antithesis, contraction, over-praise)
"Your real self is already there. The work is letting it out." (version-of-you language)
"This is the moment to unlock your full potential." (cliché, coaching register)
"You read the room well and people feel at ease around you. The work is steadying that warmth across all the moments, not just the ones that come naturally." (praises the respondent's lowest subscale, which was their first development priority; ends on the banned antithesis "not just")

# Final check before you answer

Your output is checked mechanically. Any em dash, en dash, contraction, banned phrase, exclamation mark, or question mark causes the draft to be rejected and regenerated. Before returning, reread your headline word by word:

Where you reached for an em dash, use a comma, a full stop, or a colon instead. Where you wrote a contraction, write the words in full. Where a sentence makes its point by saying what something is not, delete the negative half and state what it is.

Return only the headline. No quotation marks. No preamble. No explanation. One short sentence or two.

goal_setting._meta: Goal-setting exercise. Adapted from solution-focused scaling. One exercise per priority subscale, five steps each. Designed for printable / fillable use after the four-week plan.

intro_page.title: Where you are, and the next step up
intro_paragraphs: The two exercises that follow take each of your priority subscales in turn and walk you through five short steps. The exercises come from a method called solution-focused scaling, which has a long track record in coaching and therapy. The structure is built to do three things at once: anchor where you are, gather the evidence of what is already working, and produce one specific next step.

Each exercise takes about ten minutes. Read the description of the subscale at the top of each page first. It paints what moving up one level on that scale would look like for the people around you. That picture is what step four asks you to imagine for yourself.

Two principles before you start. First, the number you give yourself does not matter very much. A 4 from one person and a 7 from another tell you nothing on their own. What matters is the direction. Moving from a 4 to a 5 is the point of the exercise, and the four steps after the rating are what makes the move possible.

Second, treat 10 as the desired situation, not the perfect one. Perfection is a trap. Desired is workable. Aim for the version of this subscale that would meaningfully improve your life and your relationships, not for an unreachable ideal.

step_titles.step_4: What changes if you move up?
step_titles.step_5: What is the next small step?

step_prompts.step_1_lead: Where would you rate yourself on this subscale right now, on a scale of 0 to 10?
step_2_prompts: What are you already doing in this area that you would say is working?
What can you do more of, because it works?
step_3_prompts: What got you to this point on the scale, rather than a lower one?
What is different now compared to when this skill was less developed for you?
step_4_prompts: If you moved up one point on this scale, what would be different for the people around you?
What would they notice in you, that they do not notice now?
step_5_prompts: What is the smallest specific action you could take this week to move up one point?
How will you know that you have moved up the scale?

goal_setting.closing_paragraph: Come back to these two pages in four weeks. Re-rate yourself on each scale. The shift in the number is the second piece of evidence. The first is the change you and the people around you have noticed in real conversations. If the number has moved, the work is doing its job. If it has not, the next move is to look at the actions you committed to in step five and ask what stopped them from happening.

front.title: The point of all this
paragraphs: The point is to make the best of who you already are, not to change your personality. To help you become more consistent, more visible, and a more positive influence on the people around you.

The model this report rests on is straightforward. Charisma is not a fixed personality trait. It is a set of specific skills, each one improvable on its own, with practice that can be done in the real situations of the next four weeks. The two priority subscales identified in this report are where to start. The methods near the back are the patterns to reach for. The four-week plan and the goal-setting exercises are small enough to actually run.

back.title: One last thing
paragraphs: Charisma at its useful best is not about you. It is about the effect you have on the people around you. The version of you that turns up reliably, that listens well, that says the difficult thing kindly, that notices the room, that follows up on the small things. None of those is a personality trait. All of them are practices that can be built.

Pick one priority subscale. Work on it for the four weeks. Notice what changes for the people around you, and what changes for you. Then come back to the second one. Slow improvement on specific skills is what produces the version of yourself you would actually want to be.

If you would value going further, the companion book, Open-Source Charisma, sets out the full model with stories, characters, and ten practical chapters of practice. For workshops, coaching, or licensed use of the Pro instrument with your team or clients, contact Jim at jim.harvey@themessagebusiness.com. Go well.

personal_impact.intro: Personal Impact measures whether your message lands. Not whether you are confident or warm, but whether the thing you most need a person to take away actually gets through. It runs as a separate reading because the substance and the delivery are two different skills. A person can have a great deal to say and lose it in the telling. Another can hold a room with very little underneath. This score is about the telling.

components.message_craft: how the message is built: finding the one thing that matters, making it concrete, and cutting everything that buries it.
components.voice_presence: how the message is carried: pace, emphasis, and the nerve to leave a short silence after a point rather than rushing past it.

Lands reliably.what_this_suggests: Your message gets through in most rooms, to most people, most of the time. You find the thing that matters and you deliver it so it carries. This is a real strength and a rare one. Most people are stronger on substance than on getting it across. The development edge is to keep this working under pressure and in the rooms where the stakes are highest, which is exactly where delivery tends to slip.

Lands in most rooms.what_this_suggests: Your message gets through in familiar settings, with some loss in harder ones. The craft is mostly there. What varies is consistency: the same point that lands cleanly in a one-to-one can thin out in a larger room or under time pressure. The work is to notice where the loss happens and to bring the same deliberate delivery to those moments that you bring to the easy ones.

Inconsistent.what_this_suggests: Your message gets through some of the time. Often the substance is there and the delivery loses it. This is common and very fixable, because the gap is in the telling rather than the thinking. The two parts below show you where the loss is happening: whether the point is getting buried before it leaves your mouth, or whether it is the delivery that flattens it on the way out.

Not yet landing.what_this_suggests: Your message is not reliably getting through, even when the underlying thinking is sound. That last part matters: this is not a comment on your ideas. It is a comment on the channel between your ideas and the people who need them. The good news is that craft and delivery are both learnable, and small changes here tend to produce visible results quickly. The two parts below show you where to start.

personal_impact.multiplier_overrun: Your Personal Impact score is high, but your Social Skills sit below the higher band. That combination is worth naming plainly. Impact built on delivery rather than on genuine connection is polish, and a room will eventually see through it. The work is not more delivery. It is the social skills underneath: the listening, the warmth, the consistency that give the delivery something real to carry. Read this score as a prompt to strengthen the foundation, not to add more shine.
personal_impact.multiplier_sound: Your Personal Impact rests on a solid social foundation. The delivery is carrying real substance, which is what makes it land rather than merely impress. The development edge here is consistency: making sure the message lands as reliably in the hard rooms as it does in the easy ones.

page1.title: What we mean by charisma
paras: Listening with fascination. Asking the next-level question, the one that shows the other person you want to understand them properly. Listening before speaking. Checking on how someone is feeling, and meaning it. Giving tough feedback in a way that shows respect and concern for another human being.

These are the behaviours that produce what most people experience as charisma. They are simple human skills, available to anyone who decides to use them. When somebody does them well, the effect on the people around them is powerful enough to feel almost magical. The room around that person feels different. The conversations they are in go further than expected. The relationships they build last longer than other people's.

The reason the effect can feel magical, and the reason it is relatively rare, is that it requires the consistent application of a small number of simple principles as the basis for every human interaction. We call the approach Open-Source Charisma. It works the same way open source computer code works. Once you have the code, you can build almost anything with it. Without the code, everything is a challenge. Most people in working life are running without the code. They produce charismatic moments occasionally, by instinct or by effort, but they cannot do it reliably, because the underlying principles have never been made explicit to them. The popular version of the word: natural magnetism, an aura, the gift some people seem to be born with, points at the same effect, without naming the mechanism that produces it.

The rest of this report is the charisma code made clear when applied to you. We measure the behaviours that produce your charismatic effect in two parts: Confidence, how you carry yourself, and Social Skills, how you connect with the people around you. We will look at each of those in detail later in the report. First, your results.

page2.title: The two dimensions
intro: Confidence and Social Skills are the two elements that combine in the charisma code. Why? Because almost every behaviour that produces a charismatic effect on others comes from one of the two elements, or from the way the two combine.
confidence: Confidence is the internal settled sense that you are competent, capable and worthy of your place in any situation. It stems from our self-esteem and is built on our life experience and learning. Confidence is read by the people around us through the external presentation of that internal sense, through what they see and feel in how you connect with them, how you stand, how you speak, and how you respond in the moment.

Confidence is not just the strong voice of the actor or the power handshake of a President, the dominant presence of a leader in a room or the unbreakable certainty of a stand-up comedian. Confidence comes in many forms and tends to be a stable, responsive, empathetic presence at all times. It is always in good faith, never manipulative. It is a truthful, humble reaction to every situation. And Confidence does not always win. But it is the foundation of charisma because it is truthful. We measure Confidence across five specific subscales, each one describing a different facet of a person's impact. The five subscales are introduced later in the report, with your scores clearly described for each.
social_skills: Social Skills describes how you connect with the people around you. It is how you share your attention, how well you listen, your warmth, your social courtesy, and your willingness to put the other person at the centre of every interaction. Listening with fascination, asking interesting questions, caring how someone is feeling, all sit in this dimension.

Social Skills are not about fake friendliness, the warm greeting that does not last the conversation. The most socially skilled people in life are those of us whose warmth and attention are available to everyone we meet, whatever the occasion, not just the people we like or need. We measure Social Skills across five specific subscales, each one describing a different element of how you connect with the people around you. The five subscales are introduced later in the report, with your specific scores for each.
page2.combine_head: Why both, and how they combine
combine: Confidence and Social Skills combine to produce your unique charismatic approach. They tend to balance and multiply each other.

Confidence without Social Skills can produce presence without a real human connection, and can seem fake or manipulative to others. The person may appear impressive, but the room may not warm to them. Social Skills without the right level of Confidence can produce connection without real impact. The person may be warm and well-liked, but might lack the impact their substance deserves. The highest charismatic effect occurs where Confidence and Social Skills are working together.

The hypothesis of the Open-Source body of work is that most people want to be more charismatic, and that the route to it is not where they think it is. Think of charisma like the Sistine Chapel. People walk in and gape at Michelangelo's enduring brilliance. They forget that the whole building, from the ground up, is what holds the ceiling in place. Yes, the ceiling is astonishing. But the walls hold it up.

Most books on charisma teach the visible moves: the entrance, the handshake, the voice, the line you should rehearse. That work is productive in itself, and it will help build something. The trouble is that surface-only charisma can run thin when the pressure rises. The first time something goes wrong, the polished moves can stop working, because the foundations are not in place to make them last. The room reads the gap, and the version of you they remember can become the one that fell short.

The charismatic effect other people see is the ceiling. The walls are your conversational skills, your listening, your presence, your ability to find empathy with even the most challenging people. The foundations are your self-esteem, your respect for others, and the settled belief that you are worth your place in any room. You will get practical, immediate fixes from this report, but more importantly, the suggestions will help you build lasting impact from the ground up, for a lasting effect on how you meet and present yourself to the world. Every conversation you handle well, every moment of full attention you give somebody, every difficult thing you say with respect and care, flows back into your experience and builds your self-esteem and Confidence over time. The architecture is the same at every level. The more skilled and experienced might find themselves working on the same issues but at finer resolution, with smaller and harder gains. The architecture is the same.

page3.title: Your profile in detail
intro: The report produces four readings of your charismatic profile. Two of them come from the Confidence and Social Skills dimensions on the previous page. The other two pick up things the dimensions cannot see on their own. Together, the four are four ways of stress-testing the structure of your charisma. They tell you what is already holding up, where you have room to develop, and whether your visible charisma is doing the work it could be doing.

readings.head: Your Confidence score
paras: Your Confidence score is the audit of the foundations and the way you carry yourself into every room. The score is built from five subscales that measure different aspects of how you operate under your own weight: your self-esteem, your resilience and composure when pressure rises, your willingness to say the difficult thing, your appetite for growing and adapting, and your awareness of yourself in the situations you are in. The score ranges from 0 to 100, and is also banded as Lower, Developing, or Higher to help you read it in relative terms.

readings.head: Your Social Skills score
paras: Your Social Skills score is the audit of your everyday work of connecting with the people around you. The score is built from five subscales that measure the behaviours that make others feel heard, valued, and treated with respect: your empathy and listening, your warmth and social courtesy, your conversational skill, your emotional control and humility, and the authentic quality of how you show up. The score ranges from 0 to 100.

readings.head: Your Charismatic Consistency Index
paras: Your Charismatic Consistency Index picks up something the two dimension scores cannot see on their own. It measures how consistently your warmth, attention and presence are available across the different people and situations you encounter. Consistency matters to you because it affects how you feel in the full breadth of your life. It also affects how other people respond to you in those different situations. Pressure can make us give less of ourselves in certain situations and with certain people. The Index identifies where this happens for you, and points at where the work of building a more consistent charismatic impact will most repay your attention. The reading is interpreted in positive terms: higher scores describe a more consistent charismatic reach.

readings.head: Your Personal Impact
paras: Your Personal Impact is the second reading that picks up something the dimensions cannot see alone. It measures whether the visible you in the company is as effective as you want to be. People with stronger communication skills tend to have a more charismatic effect than people with less skill in those specific areas of speaking, meeting, and engaging with individuals and groups. So we measure those skills separately. Personal Impact has two components. Message Craft reads the substance: how well you structure what you want to say in formal and informal settings. Voice and Presence reads your delivery, and your ability to notice how people respond. A person with higher levels of Confidence and Social Skills can easily have a lower Personal Impact reading, and it is useful to know, because it helps them identify specific ways that they can sharpen those skills for immediate effect. The reading is reported as a 0 to 100 score, with the two components shown alongside it.

page3.together_head: How to read the four together
together: These are four lenses on the same structure. The Confidence and Social Skills scores tell you your charismatic strengths and development areas. The Charismatic Consistency Index tells you how consistently you appear across all areas of your life. The Personal Impact reading tells you how the most visible element of your charisma can be sharpened, even if you already score highly. Together, they produce the most complete picture of your charismatic profile available to you, and they point at the specific places where the next development work will most repay your attention.
Your profile on one page comes next. Then the two dimensions in detail, and the map they combine into.

page4.title: The four positions
intro: Plotted against each other, Confidence and Social Skills produce a simple map with four characteristic positions. Each position describes a different way the two dimensions can combine in working life, and a different kind of development opportunity. None of the four is a verdict. They are descriptions of where you currently operate, and from where the next step forward begins.

positions.name: Courteously Charismatic
paras: The position most people associate with the word charisma. People here come across as confident and warm at the same time. They take up the space they need without taking up the space others need. They are easy to be around, and the room tends to leave their company a little stronger than it arrived. The development edge at this position is subtle: the small contexts where the warmth might narrow, the high-pressure moments where composure might thin, the temptation to take the strengths for granted rather than to keep building on them.

positions.name: Unknowingly Influential
paras: People here connect easily and read others well. The Social Skills work is already doing what it should. The Confidence has further to come, often because the person underestimates what they are bringing to the room. The development edge is the inner work that closes the gap between the version of you the room sees, and the version of you that you give yourself credit for being. People at this position are often liked and trusted, and sometimes feel overlooked when the credit is being shared out or opportunities appear.

positions.name: Occasionally Overconfident
paras: People here carry themselves well and operate with conviction. The room reads them as capable, decisive, and present. The Social Skills work is the development edge: the warmth, listening, and willingness to put the other person at the centre of the interaction that turns presence into a truly charismatic connection. People at this position are sometimes admired and have the opportunity to grow even more. The work is to bring the same level of skill to the relationships, empathy and listening as to their outward communication.

positions.name: Incidentally Invisible
paras: People here are present, competent, and quietly underestimated by the rooms they operate in. Both dimensions have room to develop, and the development sequence is the same as for everyone else: start with the Social Skills of being present, being seen and being heard. People at this position often turn out to have a great deal more to give than the room currently sees. The development opportunity is readily achievable and can offer the fastest path to a more impactful and charismatic presence across all kinds of situations.

page4.closing_head: How to read your own position
closing: The position you occupy now is a snapshot, not a diagnosis. A starting point, not a final reading. People move through the quadrants over time as their skills, experience, and self-esteem develop. The map is a way of telling you what is already working and where the next step is most likely to repay your attention. We will show you your position on the next page.

consistency_page.title: Your Charismatic Consistency
consistency_page.concept_intro_head: A note on the concept before what your score is telling us.
concept: The Charismatic Consistency Index does not measure whether you are an authentic person. It measures something more specific and more useful: how widely your warmth, attention and presence are available across the different audiences you encounter in your life. The higher your score, the more reliably the version of you that turns up with people who matter to you also turns up with people who do not.

This is not a question of character. It is a question of reach. Most people are warm, attentive and present with their closest colleagues, the clients they already value, the friends they trust.

The interesting question is what happens at the fringes of that group. The junior colleague you only see in passing. The supplier on the phone you do not need anything specific from. The person two grades above you who you do not yet know. The Index measures whether the version of you they meet is the same version your closest colleagues meet, or a thinner, more functional version of it.
consistency_page.case_head: Now what this score is telling us in your case.
extend: Wherever you sit on the Index, the development move is the same in shape. Notice the audiences where your warmth narrows, name what it narrows to, and decide whether you want that to be the version of you those audiences experience. The narrowing is rarely deliberate. It is usually a function of tiredness, time pressure, perceived stakes, or unfamiliarity. The work is to bring the same principle of warmth into those contexts even when the surface adapts. The surface can change to fit the room. The principle underneath does not have to.

bands.charismatically_adaptable: Your warmth, attention and presence turn up reliably regardless of who is in the room. Junior or senior, familiar or new, easy room or difficult one, people experience a recognisably similar version of you. This is naturally occurring warmth at its widest reach. It is one of the most valuable working assets you have, because it builds the kind of reputation other people describe in your absence. The development edge here is small but worth naming: keep noticing the rare contexts where your warmth might narrow, even when nobody around you would mention it.
bands.broadly_adaptable: Your warmth and presence are strong across most audiences, with one or two specific contexts where the fuller version of you narrows. Naturally occurring warmth is available to most of the people you meet; in a small number of contexts it is harder to find. Most people in this band can describe the narrowing when they reflect on it: a particular kind of meeting, a particular kind of person, a particular state. The reach is already wide. The opportunity is to identify the one or two contexts where it is not, and extend the same warmth into them deliberately. The work is small and specific, and the return is out of all proportion to the effort.
bands.context_specific: Your warmth and presence are strongly available in familiar contexts, and noticeably narrower in unfamiliar or higher-stakes ones. This is not a failing. It is a common shape. People in this band are usually entirely warm and attentive with the people they feel most engaged and comfortable with. The development opportunity is to bring the same quality of presence to the audiences at the fringes of your life, even where your naturally occurring warmth is harder to find. The surface behaviours can adapt to fit each context. The underlying presence and warmth can extend further than it currently does with practice and awareness.
bands.highly_context_specific: Your warmth, attention and presence turn up most strongly in the contexts where you feel most engaged and comfortable, and noticeably less in others. This is genuinely worth working on, and the work is more rewarding than it is hard. Most people in this band are not cold in any general sense. They are highly warm with the audiences that draw their warmth naturally, and more functional with everyone else. The opportunity is to recognise that the audiences at the fringes of your life are still real audiences, and the version of you they meet is the version that builds (or does not build) your reputation in their view of the world. The methods later in this report will help. The work is to extend the naturally occurring warmth you already have, with practice and awareness, into the contexts where it does not yet appear.

ask-fuller-picture.name: Ask for the fuller picture
ask-fuller-picture.summary: When a hard piece of feedback is sitting with you, go back to the person and ask for more, so you are acting on the whole picture rather than a half-message. Most people soften feedback or stop halfway because they do not want to cause pain, which leaves you carrying uncertainty into the next interaction. The skill is asking better questions: send one or two specific prompts in advance, and after difficult feedback ask "can you say more about that?" and listen without defending.

full.issue: Feedback often arrives incomplete. People soften it or stop halfway because they do not want to cause pain. You act on a partial picture and the real issue stays unresolved. This leaves you carrying uncertainty into the next interaction and costs trust on both sides.
full.thinking: Most of us are not naturally good at giving clear feedback. The receiver who asks better questions helps the giver do their job well. This small habit turns vague comments into usable information and shows you can handle the truth.
actions: Send the person one or two specific prompts in advance: "What is one thing I could do differently to be more effective?" or "What do people better at this than me tend to do?"
After any difficult feedback, ask: "Can you say more about that?" and listen without defending.
Follow up a few days later: "I tried X based on what you said, how does it land now?"
full.source: Draws from David Maister's work on trusted relationships and common feedback practice in executive coaching.

ask-next-level-by-default.name: Ask the next-level question by default
ask-next-level-by-default.summary: Conversations often stay on the surface: you hear the first answer and move on, so the person never reaches what they really needed to say. People rarely say exactly what they mean the first time, and a genuine follow-up gives them space and signals real interest. Make "what else?" or "say more about that" your default, pause two full seconds before you speak, and pick one detail they mentioned to ask about specifically.

full.issue: Conversations often stay on the surface. You hear the first answer and move on, so the person never reaches what they really needed to say. The exchange feels polite but not valuable, and connection stays thin.
full.thinking: People rarely say exactly what they mean first time. A genuine follow-up question gives them space and signals that you are interested in the real story, not just the polite version. This is where trust and understanding grow.
actions: Make "What else?" or "Say more about that" your default follow-up.
After they answer, pause for two full seconds before you speak. Use the silence.
Pick one detail they mentioned and ask a specific question about it: "You said the meeting felt tense, what was the hardest part?"
full.source: Consistent with active listening practices in Carl Rogers' person-centred approach and Fritz Perls' emphasis on layers of expression.

colleague-test.name: The colleague test
colleague-test.summary: When something goes wrong, it is easy to turn one setback into a verdict on your whole worth. You would never judge a capable colleague that way after a single difficult meeting, so apply the same fairness to yourself. Pause, name the specific thing that did not land, and ask: "What would I tell a colleague I respect in the same position?" Then give yourself that measured view. It stops the story spreading and keeps the learning useful rather than personal.

full.issue: One setback quickly becomes a verdict on your whole worth. You judge yourself more harshly than you would ever judge a capable colleague. This swings your confidence and makes other people manage your mood instead of working with you.
full.thinking: Self-compassion is not softness. It is applying the same fairness you extend to others. When your baseline stays steady, people experience you as reliable rather than reactive.
actions: After a difficult moment, ask: "What would I tell a colleague I respect in the same spot?" and follow your own advice.
Write one sentence separating the event from your identity: "The meeting went badly. I am still the same person who handled last week's project well."
At the end of a hard day, note one thing that went right, however small.

own-verdict-first.name: Your own verdict first
own-verdict-first.summary: Before you look for anyone else's opinion on work you have done, form your own clear reading of it. Write one sentence on what went well, what could be better, and what you learned, and only then seek other views. This gives your own judgement something solid to stand on when feedback arrives, and reduces the swing between external praise and criticism. People notice when your sense of yourself is not hostage to the last person who spoke.

full.issue: You wait for other people to confirm that your work was good before you believe it. This leaves your sense of worth in their hands and makes praise feel temporary and criticism feel crushing.
full.thinking: Real confidence includes trusting your own eyes. Forming your own view first gives you a stable place to stand when external feedback arrives.
actions: After finishing a piece of work, write one sentence: "What I did well was..." before you ask anyone else.
Keep a short private log of your own verdicts on weekly work. Review it monthly.
When praise comes, note your own view first, then add the external comment.

ask-permission-to-differ.name: Ask permission to differ
ask-permission-to-differ.summary: When you see a problem or hold a different view, especially with someone senior, open with a one-line pre-frame: "Can I offer a different read on this?" It signals respect, lowers defences, and makes the difficult thing easier for both sides to hear. Follow it immediately with the point, kept short and specific. The small courtesy keeps the room open and raises the chance your view is taken seriously rather than dismissed as pushback.

full.issue: You hold a different view but keep it to yourself, especially with senior people. The room loses your input and decisions are poorer. You stay safe but invisible.
full.thinking: A small courtesy at the start lowers defences and raises the chance your point lands. Courage with courtesy is more effective than silence or blunt force.
actions: Open with: "Can I offer a different read on this?" then state your point cleanly.
Practise the phrase in low-stakes meetings first.
Follow up afterwards: "Did that land usefully?" to learn how it was received.

say-headline-first.name: Say the headline first
say-headline-first.summary: When you have something difficult or important to say, lead with the single clear point, "the main thing is X", then explain or soften around it. Most people do the opposite, cushioning first so the real message gets lost. Stating the headline upfront honours the listener with clarity and makes action far more likely. The courage is already there; this simply lets the message land.

full.issue: You soften difficult messages so much that the main point disappears. People nod politely but nothing changes. The courage was there; the clarity was not.
full.thinking: Clarity is a form of respect. Leading with the single point lets the other person engage with the real issue instead of guessing.
actions: State the headline first: "The main thing is we need to change X." Then explain.
Rehearse the one-sentence version out loud before the conversation.

detail-carried-forward.name: The detail carried forward
detail-carried-forward.summary: In your next conversation, notice one specific human detail about the other person, a project they mentioned, a concern, a small win, and make a quiet note. Next time you meet, weave it in lightly: "How did that pitch with the new client go?" People feel genuinely seen when you remember what matters to them. It takes almost no effort and turns ordinary interactions into the kind that build lasting warmth and trust.

full.issue: You meet people but the small human details do not stick. They feel politely acknowledged but not genuinely known. Warmth stays shallow.
full.thinking: Remembering one specific thing signals that you were paying real attention. It turns routine interactions into the start of a relationship.
actions: In the conversation, note one non-work detail.
Next time you meet, mention it lightly and naturally.
Keep a short note on your phone after important chats.

no-ask-follow-up.name: The no-ask follow-up
no-ask-follow-up.summary: After a conversation that mattered, send a short message with nothing attached: "I was thinking about what you said about the team restructure, hope it is settling." No request, no agenda, just a sign that you were listening. These small, unconditional touches turn transactional contacts into relationships. They cost little and signal the kind of warmth people remember and return.

full.issue: Relationships fade once the task is done. People sense the contact was transactional and pull back.
full.thinking: A message with nothing attached shows the relationship matters beyond what they can do for you. This builds the kind of trust that lasts.
actions: After a good conversation, send: "I was thinking about what you said about..."
Do it within a week while it is still fresh.
Make it a habit for one person per week.

offer-as-view.name: Offer it as a view, not a verdict
offer-as-view.summary: When you share a strong opinion, frame it as one perspective among others, "my read on this is..." or "in my experience...", rather than settled fact. It keeps the room open for other people to contribute without feeling they must fight or agree. The conversation stays richer, decisions get better information, and you come across as confident but not dominating.

full.issue: You state opinions as facts. The room closes down or prepares to fight. Good thinking stops.
full.thinking: Framing your view as one perspective invites others in. The conversation stays alive and decisions improve.
actions: Say "My read on this is..." or "In my experience..."
Ask "What do others think?" straight after.
Notice when you slip into certainty and soften the next sentence.

credit-on-the-spot.name: Credit on the spot
credit-on-the-spot.summary: When praise comes your way for something that involved others, name their contribution in the same moment: "Sarah did the heavy lifting on the numbers, I just pulled it together." Do it publicly and immediately. Credit given on the spot lands as genuine humility and confidence; delayed or private credit feels like an afterthought. People notice who shares the light, and it builds trust faster than almost anything else.

full.issue: You accept praise without naming others who contributed. It feels like taking more than your share and quietly erodes trust.
full.thinking: Public, immediate credit shows humility and confidence. People remember who shared the light.
actions: In the moment of praise, name the contribution: "Sarah did the heavy lifting on the numbers."
Practise it even when it feels slightly awkward.
Make it specific and genuine.

speak-last-top-seat.name: Speak last from the top seat
speak-last-top-seat.summary: When you are the most senior or experienced person in the room, hold your view until everyone else has spoken. Say something like "I would like to hear from everyone first." You get their real thinking instead of managed agreement, the discussion is richer, and people feel genuinely included. The discipline also sharpens your own listening.

full.issue: As the senior person you speak first. Others manage their input and you miss their real thinking.
full.thinking: Holding your view until last gives the room permission to think freely. You get better information and stronger commitment.
actions: Say: "I'd like to hear from everyone first."
Take notes while others speak.
Summarise what you heard before adding your view.

low-energy-warmth-baseline.name: The low-energy warmth baseline
low-energy-warmth-baseline.summary: On the days when your energy is low, set a minimum standard you still meet: a genuine greeting, full attention in conversations, remembering one detail about the other person. Decide in advance what that baseline looks like, and protect it even when you feel least like it. The version of you that shows up on tired days is often the one people remember most, and a reliable minimum prevents the drop that others notice.

full.issue: On low-energy days your warmth drops. People remember the tired version of you more than the good days.
full.thinking: Consistency matters more than perfection. A reliable minimum standard protects your reputation on the days that test it.
actions: Decide your baseline in advance (genuine greeting, full attention, one remembered detail).
Protect it even when you feel least like it.
Shorten meetings or slow your pace if needed to maintain quality.
